116473.e: In 2018 Hawaii decided to ban the sale of sunscreens with these two filters. The ban came into force in 2021 because the substances might harm corals.
116473.m: Some UV filters are suspected of harming corals.

116474.q: Why is titanium dioxide often used as nanoparticles in sun creams?
a: Finer particles leave less of a white film
116474.e: Large pigment particles also scatter visible light and make the skin look white. Very small particles are almost transparent but still filter UV.
116474.m: Nanoparticles make mineral sun cream more transparent.

116475.q: In the EU, what is the highest permitted sun protection factor label on sunscreens?
116475.e: According to an EU recommendation, products with very high protection are labelled “50+”. Higher numbers would suggest an extra benefit that hardly exists.
116475.m: The highest sun protection factor on EU labels is 50+.

116476.q: What causes the immediate pigmentation shortly after UVA exposure?
a: Melanin already present is oxidised and darkens
Blood builds up in the skin
116476.e: In immediate pigmentation no new melanin is made. Existing pigment precursors are oxidised by UVA, and the colour usually fades again quickly.
116476.m: The immediate tan only darkens pigment that is already there.

116477.q: After how long does the delayed tan from newly formed melanin become visible?
116477.e: In delayed pigmentation the melanocytes make new melanin and pass it on to the keratinocytes. This process takes a few days.
116477.m: A real tan only develops after a few days.

116478.q: Roughly how much protection does a well-developed suntan give?
a: About the same as a sun protection factor of 2 to 4
About the same as a sun protection factor of 30
About the same as a sun protection factor of 50
116478.e: A tan offers only slight natural protection. It does not replace sun cream, clothing or shade.
116478.m: Tanned skin is only weakly protected against UV.

116479.q: From a biological point of view, what does a tan show?
a: A reaction to UV damage in the skin
116479.e: Tanning is triggered when UV radiation damages the DNA of keratinocytes. Through signalling substances these cells stimulate the melanocytes to make pigment.
116479.m: A tan is a sign that the skin is defending itself against damage.

116480.q: Which cells in the skin make the pigment melanin?
116480.e: Melanocytes sit in the lowest layer of the epidermis. They make melanin and pass it on to the surrounding skin cells, which become darker as a result.
116480.m: Melanocytes make the skin pigment melanin.

116481.q: Which active ingredient in self-tanners colours the horny layer without UV radiation?
116481.e: Dihydroxyacetone reacts with amino acids in the top layer of skin to form brown compounds. This colour does not protect against UV radiation and disappears as the skin flakes off.
116481.m: Self-tanners colour the skin but do not protect against the sun.

116482.q: Which rule applies in Switzerland to the use of sunbeds by minors?
a: It is only allowed with sun cream
It is only allowed in winter
116482.e: Under the Federal Act on Protection against Dangers from Non-Ionising Radiation and Sound, young people under 18 may not use sunbeds. Their skin is considered particularly sensitive.
116482.m: In Switzerland, sunbeds are banned for minors.

116483.q: Which fashion designer is considered to have made the suntan an ideal of beauty in the 1920s?
116483.e: Before that, pale skin was considered refined in Europe. Coco Chanel appeared with a tan, and a tan became a sign of leisure and wealth.
116483.m: A tan only became an ideal of beauty in the 20th century.

116484.q: Why is it useful to know your own skin type?
a: To calculate your vitamin C needs
116484.e: The skin type shows how sensitively the skin reacts to sun. If you know it, you can adapt sun cream, clothing and time in the sun better.
116484.m: Your skin type helps you choose the right sun protection.

116485.q: How many skin types does the Fitzpatrick scale distinguish?
116485.e: The scale ranges from type I with very fair skin that always burns to type VI with deeply dark skin. There are four more levels in between.
116485.m: The Fitzpatrick scale has six skin types.

116486.q: Which feature describes Fitzpatrick skin type I?
a: Always burns and practically never tans
116486.e: People with skin type I have very fair skin, often freckles and reddish hair. They have the shortest natural protection time.
116486.m: Skin type I burns quickly and hardly tans.

116487.q: By which criterion are Fitzpatrick skin types mainly classified?
a: By how the skin reacts to sun
By the fat content of the skin
By the number of hairs per cm²
116487.e: What matters is how easily the skin gets sunburnt and how well it tans. From this its sensitivity to light can be estimated.
116487.m: Skin types describe how sensitive the skin is to sun.

116488.q: What does the term “natural protection time” of the skin mean?
a: The time without protection until sunburn begins
The time until the skin grows back
The time until sun cream soaks in
The time until a tan fades
116488.e: The natural protection time tells you how long unprotected skin can be exposed to the sun before it turns red. It depends on skin type and the UV index.
116488.m: The natural protection time is especially short for fair skin.

116489.q: A person has a natural protection time of 10 minutes and uses SPF 30 correctly. What is the theoretical maximum protection time?
116489.e: You multiply the natural protection time by the sun protection factor: 10 minutes times 30 makes 300 minutes. Experts recommend using only about two thirds of this time.
116489.m: Protection time is natural protection time times sun protection factor.

116490.q: Which skin types are especially common among people in Switzerland of central European origin?
116490.e: Many people of central European origin have fair to medium-fair skin that first burns and then tans. This corresponds to skin types II and III.
116490.m: In central Europe, skin types II and III are most common.

116491.q: Can people with skin type VI get skin cancer?
116491.e: Dark skin is better protected against UV, but not completely. In dark skin, skin cancer is also often detected late, for example on the soles of the feet.
116491.m: Even very dark skin can develop skin cancer.

116492.q: Which group of cells do the Langerhans cells of the skin belong to?
a: Dendritic cells of the immune system
Muscle cells of the hair follicle muscles
116492.e: Langerhans cells are antigen-presenting immune cells of the epidermis. With their extensions they form a dense surveillance network.
116492.m: Langerhans cells are the immune system's guards in the epidermis.

116493.q: What did Paul Langerhans first think the cells he discovered in the epidermis in 1868 were?
116493.e: Paul Langerhans described the branched cells in 1868 as a young medical student. Because of their extensions he thought they were nerve cells; their role in the immune system was only recognised about a hundred years later.
116493.m: Langerhans cells were first thought to be nerve cells.

116494.q: How do Langerhans cells keep watch over the whole epidermis even though there are only a few of them?
a: By forming a horny layer themselves
116494.e: Langerhans cells stretch their extensions out between the skin cells and so form a dense network. Under the electron microscope they can also be recognised by the tennis-racket-shaped Birbeck granules.
116494.m: Langerhans cells form a surveillance network with their extensions.

116495.q: What do Langerhans cells do after they have taken up a foreign antigen?
a: They travel to the lymph nodes and present it to T cells
They dissolve in the horny layer
116495.e: The cells process the antigen and travel through lymph vessels to the lymph nodes. There they activate T lymphocytes and start a targeted defence.
116495.m: Langerhans cells take foreign substances to the T cells.

116496.q: What effect does UV radiation have on Langerhans cells?
a: It reduces their number and function
It turns them into fat cells
116496.e: UV radiation weakens Langerhans cells and so suppresses the immune defence in the skin. This makes it easier for damaged cells to escape immune control.
116496.m: UV radiation weakens the skin's immune system.

116497.q: How are Langerhans cells made specifically visible in a skin sample under the microscope?
a: With labelled antibodies against their surface molecules
With a magnifying glass and no staining at all
116497.e: Langerhans cells carry typical molecules such as CD1a and langerin. Labelled antibodies bind to them and stain the cells specifically.
116497.m: Labelled antibodies are used to stain particular cells specifically.

116498.q: Which structures should Langerhans cells of the skin not be confused with, even though they have the same discoverer?
a: Islets of Langerhans in the pancreas
116498.e: Paul Langerhans also described groups of cells in the pancreas that make hormones such as insulin. These have nothing to do with the immune cells of the skin.
116498.m: Langerhans cells and islets of Langerhans are different things.

116499.q: In which part of the skin are Langerhans cells mainly found?
a: In the bone marrow of the skin
116499.e: Langerhans cells sit mainly in the middle layers of the epidermis. There they catch pathogens and foreign substances that get past the horny layer.
116499.m: Langerhans cells keep watch over the epidermis.

116500.q: Which layer of skin forms the most important physical barrier against water loss?
116500.e: The horny layer consists of dead, keratinised cells embedded in lipids. It stops the body losing too much water.
116500.m: The horny layer is the skin's most important barrier.

116501.q: Which model gives a clear picture of how the horny layer is built?
116501.e: The keratinised cells are the bricks, the lipids between them the mortar. Together they make a tight wall.
116501.m: The horny layer is built like a wall of bricks and mortar.

116502.q: Which group of lipids makes up a main share of the barrier lipids in the horny layer?
116502.e: The lipids between the horny cells consist mainly of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids. They arrange themselves in dense layers.
116502.m: Ceramides are important building blocks of the skin barrier.

116503.q: Roughly what pH does the acid mantle of healthy skin surface have?
116503.e: The skin surface is slightly acidic, roughly in the range pH 4.5 to 5.5. This inhibits many pathogens and supports enzymes that build the barrier.
116503.m: Healthy skin is slightly acidic on the surface.

116504.q: Which skin disease is closely linked to a disturbed skin barrier?
116504.e: In atopic eczema the skin barrier is weakened. The skin loses a lot of water, becomes dry and reacts sensitively to irritants and allergens.
116504.m: Atopic eczema goes together with a disturbed skin barrier.

116505.q: Which measurement is often used to test the function of the skin barrier?
116505.e: Transepidermal water loss measures how much water evaporates outwards through the skin. If the barrier is damaged, this value rises.
116505.m: A lot of water loss through the skin shows a disturbed barrier.

116506.q: Roughly how long does it take for the epidermis to renew itself from the basal layer to flaking off?
116506.e: New cells form in the basal layer, move upwards and become keratinised. After about four weeks they flake off at the surface.
116506.m: The epidermis renews itself about once a month.

116507.q: Why can washing very often with soap weaken the skin barrier?
a: It dissolves lipids and shifts the pH
116507.e: Surfactants dissolve skin fats out of the horny layer, and alkaline soaps raise the pH. The skin becomes dry and more prone to irritation.
116507.m: Too much soap removes the skin's fats and weakens its barrier.

116805.q: Which process does the P wave on the ECG show?
116805.e: The P wave arises when excitation spreads from the sinus node across both atria (depolarisation of the atria).
116805.m: The P wave stands for excitation of the atria.

116806.q: What does the T wave on the ECG represent?
116806.e: The T wave shows the recovery of the ventricular muscle from excitation. The spread of excitation in the ventricles, by contrast, is shown by the QRS complex.
116806.m: With the T wave the excitation of the ventricles recovers.

116807.q: What does the PQ interval on the ECG show?
a: How long the excitation takes from the atria to the ventricles
How long a whole heartbeat lasts
How much blood the heart pumps out per beat
116807.e: The PQ interval runs from the start of atrial excitation to the start of ventricular excitation. It shows how fast the excitation is passed on through the AV node.
116807.m: The PQ interval measures conduction from the atria to the ventricles.

116808.q: An ECG runs at 25 mm/s. The distance between two R waves is 20 mm. What is the heart rate?
116808.e: 20 mm divided by 25 mm/s gives 0.8 s per beat. 60 s divided by 0.8 s gives 75 beats per minute.
116808.m: You get the heart rate by dividing 60 seconds by the RR interval in seconds.

116809.q: Who received the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 1924 for developing the electrocardiogram?
116809.e: The Dutch physiologist Willem Einthoven developed the string galvanometer and with it the modern ECG. He received the Nobel Prize for this in 1924.
116809.m: Willem Einthoven is considered the father of the modern ECG.

116810.q: How many leads does a standard resting ECG include?
116810.e: The standard ECG consists of 6 limb leads (Einthoven and Goldberger) and 6 chest leads according to Wilson (V1 to V6).
116810.m: A standard resting ECG has twelve leads.

116811.q: Why is an ECG recorded immediately when a heart attack is suspected?
a: A heart attack changes the heart's electrical signals in a typical way
The ECG shows blocked arteries as a picture
The ECG measures the blood pressure in the coronary arteries
116811.e: When heart muscle dies from lack of oxygen, it conducts the excitation differently. This can often be seen at once on the ECG, for example as ST elevation.
116811.m: An ECG can quickly reveal a heart attack.

116812.q: Which part of the ECG curve shows the excitation of the ventricles?
116812.e: The QRS complex is the large, sharp spike on the ECG. It arises when excitation spreads through the powerful ventricular muscle.
116812.m: The large QRS spike stands for excitation of the ventricles.

116813.q: What does an ECG basically measure?
a: The blood pressure in the aorta
The blood flow in the veins
The heart sounds over the chest
116813.e: The excitation of heart muscle cells creates electric fields. Electrodes on the skin measure the resulting potential differences in the millivolt range.
116813.m: The ECG records the electrical activity of the heart.

116814.q: How fast does the AV node conduct excitation compared with the Purkinje fibres?
a: Not at all, it only conducts backwards
116814.e: In the AV node excitation is conducted at only a few centimetres per second, in the Purkinje fibres at a few metres per second.
116814.m: Conduction is slowest in the AV node and fastest in the Purkinje fibres.

116815.q: What happens to the heartbeat if the sinus node fails and the AV node takes over the rhythm?
116815.e: The AV node can step in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower than that of the sinus node.
116815.m: The AV node is a slower backup pacemaker of the heart.

116816.q: Between which parts of the heart does the AV node pass on the excitation?
a: From the atria to the ventricles
From the ventricles to the aorta
From the lungs to the atria
From the brain to the heart
116816.e: AV stands for atrioventricular, meaning atrium and ventricle. The AV node is the only normal electrical connection between the atria and the ventricles.
116816.m: The AV node links the atria and ventricles electrically.

116817.q: Why is the excitation briefly delayed in the AV node?
a: So that the ventricles fill before they contract
So that the heart saves energy
So that the blood pressure falls
So that the lungs get more air
116817.e: First the atria contract and pump blood into the ventricles. Only then should the ventricles contract.
116817.m: The delay in the AV node gives the ventricles time to fill.

116818.q: Which examination measures the electrical excitation of the heart?
116818.e: The ECG records the excitation of the heart using electrodes on the skin. Problems with conduction in the AV node show up as longer intervals.
116818.m: The ECG shows the electrical activity of the heart.

116819.q: How does the vagus nerve (parasympathetic system) affect the AV node?
a: It has no effect at all
It makes the AV node the pacemaker
116819.e: The parasympathetic system has a negative dromotropic effect, meaning it delays conduction in the AV node. The sympathetic system, by contrast, speeds it up.
116819.m: The vagus nerve slows conduction in the AV node.

116820.q: Why does the AV node protect the ventricles during atrial fibrillation?
a: It lets only some of the impulses through
116820.e: In atrial fibrillation very many disordered impulses arrive at the AV node. Because of its slow conduction and refractory period, only some of them reach the ventricles.
116820.m: The AV node acts like a filter for atrial impulses that are too fast.

116821.q: Where is the AV node located?
a: At the floor of the right atrium near the septum
In the tip of the left ventricle
In the wall of the aorta
At the opening of the pulmonary veins
116821.e: The AV node lies in the right atrium near the atrial septum, above the transition to the ventricles (in the so-called triangle of Koch).
116821.m: The AV node sits in the right atrium at the border between the atria and ventricles.

116822.q: In which order does normal excitation pass through the heart?
a: Sinus node, AV node, bundle of His, bundle branches, Purkinje fibres
AV node, sinus node, bundle branches, bundle of His, Purkinje fibres
Sinus node, bundle of His, AV node, Purkinje fibres, bundle branches
Purkinje fibres, bundle branches, bundle of His, AV node, sinus node
116822.e: Excitation starts in the sinus node, travels across the atria to the AV node and then via the bundle of His and the bundle branches to the Purkinje fibres in the ventricular muscle.
116822.m: Excitation runs from the sinus node via the AV node to the Purkinje fibres.

116823.q: Which structure is the primary pacemaker of the healthy heart?
116823.e: The sinus node has the highest intrinsic rate of about 60 to 80 per minute and therefore sets the rhythm.
116823.m: In the healthy heart the sinus node sets the rhythm.

116824.q: What is the role of the bundle of His in the heart?
a: It carries the excitation from the AV node to the ventricles
It creates the heart's basic rhythm
It supplies the heart muscle with blood
116824.e: The bundle of His is part of the conduction system. It carries the excitation from the AV node through the septum to the bundle branches. It is named after the Basel doctor Wilhelm His Jr.
116824.m: The bundle of His carries the excitation to the ventricles.

116825.q: What does the heart's conduction system consist of?
a: Smooth muscle cells of the blood vessels
116825.e: The conduction system consists of special heart muscle cells that can excite themselves and pass on excitation quickly. That is why the heart keeps beating even without nerves.
116825.m: The heart produces its excitation with its own specialised muscle cells.

116826.q: What takes over the rhythm if the sinus node fails?
a: The AV node, with a slower rhythm
The lungs, with their breathing rhythm
116826.e: If the sinus node fails, the AV node steps in as a backup pacemaker. However, its own rhythm of about 40 to 60 beats per minute is slower.
116826.m: If the sinus node fails, the slower AV node takes over.

116827.q: Why does the AV node briefly delay passing on the excitation?
a: So that the atria can fill the ventricles first
So that the sinus node can recover
So that the heart valves can open
So that the blood in the lungs can take up oxygen
116827.e: The short delay in the AV node makes sure the atria contract first and press blood into the ventricles. Only after that do the ventricles contract.
116827.m: The AV node briefly holds back so that the ventricles fill first.

116828.q: What is the heart's ability to produce excitation itself without an outside stimulus called?
116828.e: Pacemaker cells slowly depolarise by themselves until a threshold is reached. This property is called automaticity, or the autonomy of the heart.
116828.m: Thanks to automaticity, the heart beats under its own power.

a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
Blood volume divided by stroke volume
116829.e: Cardiac output is the amount of blood that one ventricle pumps out per minute. It is the amount per beat times the number of beats per minute.
116829.m: Cardiac output is the product of stroke volume and heart rate.

116830.q: A heart has a stroke volume of 80 ml and beats 60 times a minute. What is the cardiac output?
116830.e: 80 ml times 60 per minute makes 4,800 ml per minute, that is 4.8 litres per minute.
116830.m: For cardiac output, multiply the stroke volume by the heart rate.

116831.q: How much blood does a heart pump per day with a cardiac output of 5 l/min?
116831.e: A day has 24 times 60, that is 1,440 minutes. 1,440 times 5 litres makes 7,200 litres.
116831.m: The heart pumps several thousand litres of blood every day.

116832.q: During exercise an athlete has a stroke volume of 150 ml and a heart rate of 180 per minute. What is his cardiac output?
116832.e: 150 ml times 180 per minute makes 27,000 ml per minute, that is 27 litres per minute.
116832.m: During exercise, cardiac output can rise to several times the resting value.

116833.q: Roughly how large is the cardiac output of a healthy adult at rest?
116833.e: At rest, a healthy adult's heart pumps out about 5 litres of blood per minute. That is roughly the body's entire amount of blood.
116833.m: At rest the heart pumps about five litres of blood per minute.

116834.q: How does the heart increase its cardiac output during physical exercise?
a: Through higher stroke volume and higher heart rate
Only through a lower heart rate
116834.e: During exercise the heart beats faster and pumps out more blood per beat. Together these greatly increase the amount of blood per minute.
116834.m: More beats and more blood per beat increase cardiac output.

116835.q: Cardiac output can be calculated as oxygen uptake divided by the difference in oxygen between arterial and venous blood. What is it at 250 ml/min and 50 ml per litre of blood?
116835.e: 250 ml/min divided by 50 ml/l gives 5 l/min. This method is called the Fick principle.
116835.m: According to Fick, you divide the oxygen uptake by the arteriovenous difference.

116836.q: What does the cardiac index show?
a: Cardiac output per square metre of body surface
Heart rate per kilogram of body weight
Stroke volume per litre of blood
116836.e: The cardiac index relates cardiac output to body surface area. This makes it easier to compare large and small people.
116836.m: The cardiac index makes cardiac output comparable between people of different sizes.

116837.q: The end-diastolic volume is 130 ml and the end-systolic volume is 60 ml. What is the stroke volume?
116837.e: The stroke volume is the difference between the filling at the end of diastole and the remaining volume at the end of systole: 130 ml minus 60 ml makes 70 ml.
116837.m: Stroke volume is end-diastolic minus end-systolic volume.

116838.q: The stroke volume is 60 ml and the end-diastolic volume is 120 ml. What is the ejection fraction?
116838.e: The ejection fraction is the stroke volume divided by the end-diastolic volume: 60 divided by 120 gives 0.5, that is 50 %.
116838.m: The ejection fraction shows what share of the filling is pumped out.

116839.q: What does the Frank-Starling mechanism state?
a: Greater filling leads to a larger stroke volume
A higher heart rate always lowers stroke volume
The heart always pumps the same amount of blood
The sinus node adapts to blood pressure
116839.e: If the ventricle is filled and stretched more during diastole, it then contracts more strongly. In this way the heart automatically adapts to changing return of blood.
116839.m: According to Frank-Starling, a fuller heart pumps out more blood.

116840.q: What is meant by the afterload of the heart?
a: The resistance to pumping out blood
The filling of the ventricle before contraction
The blood left behind after the beat
116840.e: Afterload is the force the ventricle has to overcome when pumping out blood, mainly the pressure in the aorta. If it rises, stroke volume falls with the same force.
116840.m: Afterload is the resistance the heart pumps against.

116841.q: Roughly how large is the stroke volume of a healthy adult at rest?
116841.e: At rest each ventricle pumps out about 70 ml of blood per beat, and much more in trained people.
116841.m: At rest each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per beat.

116842.q: Why do endurance athletes often have a low resting heart rate?
a: Their cardiac output is much smaller
116842.e: A trained heart is stronger and pumps out more blood per beat. So it needs fewer beats per minute for the same cardiac output.
116842.m: A larger stroke volume allows a lower resting heart rate.

116843.q: How do you calculate cardiac output, the amount of blood the heart pumps per minute?
a: Stroke volume divided by heart rate
116843.e: With 70 ml per beat and 70 beats per minute, the heart pumps about 4.9 litres of blood per minute.
116843.m: Cardiac output equals stroke volume times heart rate.

116844.q: What is called the preload of the heart?
a: The stretch of the ventricle at the end of filling
The number of heartbeats per minute
The resistance in the lung vessels
116844.e: Preload corresponds to the filling and stretching of the ventricle at the end of diastole. It depends mainly on the return of blood through the veins.
116844.m: Preload is the stretching of the ventricle by the incoming blood.

116845.q: Where do the coronary arteries arise?
a: From the root of the aorta
116845.e: The two coronary arteries branch off the aorta just above the aortic valve. In this way they are the first to receive oxygen-rich blood.
116845.m: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta just above the aortic valve.

117304.q: Why is the door handle placed as far as possible from the hinges?
a: A long lever arm needs less force
It makes the door close faster
117304.e: For the same turning effect, a smaller force is enough if you are further from the pivot. That is why a door is easy to open at its outer edge.
117304.m: A long lever arm saves force.

117642.q: What do people with severe beta thalassaemia (thalassaemia major) usually need for their whole life?
117642.e: In the severe form, hardly any working haemoglobin is made. The patients, whose condition used to be called Cooley's anaemia, therefore need donated blood regularly.
117642.m: Severe thalassaemia requires regular blood transfusions.

117643.q: What problem do many blood transfusions cause in thalassaemia patients?
117643.e: Every transfusion brings iron that the body can hardly get rid of; that is why iron chelators such as deferasirox are needed.
117643.m: Many transfusions overload the body with iron.

117644.q: What kind of disease is thalassaemia?
a: A result of too little iron in food
An autoimmune disease of the spleen
117644.e: Thalassaemias are caused by changes in the genes for the globin chains of haemoglobin. They are passed on from parents to children.
117644.m: Thalassaemia is an inherited disorder of haemoglobin production.

117645.q: Which lab value helps to tell mild thalassaemia apart from iron deficiency?
117645.e: Both show small, pale red blood cells, but in thalassaemia the storage iron ferritin is normal or raised, while in iron deficiency it is low.
117645.m: A normal ferritin level argues against iron deficiency.

117646.q: Why is thalassaemia especially common in the Mediterranean region?
a: Carriers are somewhat better protected against malaria
The warm climate damages blood production
The diet contains too little iron
117646.e: People who carry only one altered copy of the gene are hardly ill, but are somewhat better protected against severe malaria. In former malaria areas such as the Mediterranean, the trait therefore spread.
117646.m: Thalassaemia carriers are better protected against malaria.

117647.q: Which protein forms a net of threads at the end of blood clotting that closes the wound?
117647.e: At the end of the clotting cascade, soluble fibrinogen is converted into fibrin. The fibrin threads form a net in which blood cells get caught.
117647.m: Fibrin threads make the blood clot stable.

117648.q: Which blood components are the first to stick to a wound and form a plug?
117648.e: Platelets (thrombocytes) stick to the damaged vessel wall and clump together. Clotting then stabilises the plug with fibrin.
117648.m: Platelets are the first to seal a wound.

117649.q: Which vitamin does the liver need to make several clotting factors?
117649.e: Without vitamin K, the liver cannot finish making several clotting factors. Some blood thinners work by blocking vitamin K.
117649.m: Vitamin K is needed for blood clotting.

117650.q: Which ion is essential for the cascade as clotting factor IV?
117650.e: Calcium ions link clotting factors to phospholipid surfaces, for example on activated platelets; without them the cascade stalls.

117651.q: What is the name of the mostly inherited disease in which blood clots poorly because a clotting factor is missing?
117651.e: In haemophilia, usually factor VIII or IX is missing. Even small injuries can bleed for a long time.

117652.q: Which enzyme dissolves blood clots during fibrinolysis?
117652.e: Plasmin is formed from plasminogen, for example by tissue plasminogen activator, and breaks down fibrin.

117653.q: Why do some people take so-called blood thinners?
a: To prevent blood clots such as thromboses
To make more red blood cells
To make their blood runnier for donating
117653.e: Blood thinners slow down clotting. They prevent dangerous clots from forming in vessels or in the heart, for example after a thrombosis.
117653.m: Blood thinners protect against dangerous blood clots.

117654.q: What happens first to the affected blood vessel when you are injured?
117654.e: The smooth muscle of the vessel wall contracts immediately. That way less blood flows out until platelets and clotting close the wound.

117655.q: What is the main job of thrombin in blood clotting?
117655.e: Thrombin cuts small peptides off fibrinogen, after which the fibrin monomers join together into threads.

117656.q: From which inactive precursor is thrombin formed?
117656.e: Prothrombin (factor II) is split into thrombin (factor IIa) by the prothrombinase complex made of factors Xa and Va.

117657.q: What kind of enzyme is thrombin?
117657.e: Thrombin is a protease: it cuts proteins at specific points, for example fibrinogen. More precisely, it belongs to the serine proteases.

117658.q: Which inhibitor made by the body inactivates thrombin and is strongly boosted by heparin?
117658.e: Antithrombin binds thrombin and factor Xa; heparin speeds up this inhibition many times over.
117658.m: Antithrombin blocks thrombin, and heparin boosts it.

117659.q: Why does the body have, besides thrombin, substances that slow down clotting?
a: So that clots stay limited to the injured spot
So that the blood can carry more oxygen
So that more red blood cells are made
117659.e: Without brakes, clotting would spread through the whole vascular system. Inhibitors such as antithrombin or the protein C system on the vessel wall make sure clots only form where they are needed.
117659.m: Inhibitors keep clotting limited to the wound.

117660.q: Which substance in leech saliva blocks thrombin directly?
117660.e: Hirudin is a strong direct thrombin inhibitor; medicines such as bivalirudin were developed based on it.
117660.m: Hirudin from the leech blocks thrombin.

117661.q: What are medicines that block thrombin used for?
117661.e: Thrombin inhibitors such as dabigatran are among the so-called blood thinners. They protect, for example, against thromboses, pulmonary embolisms or strokes in atrial fibrillation.
117661.m: Thrombin inhibitors protect against dangerous blood clots.

117662.q: Thrombin activates clotting factors, which in turn produce more thrombin. What is such a principle called?
117662.e: Thrombin activates factors V, VIII and XI, among others, which boost its own production. This positive feedback makes clotting start like an avalanche.
117662.m: Thrombin boosts its own production through positive feedback.

117663.q: Which form makes up most cases of haemophilia?
117663.e: Around 80 to 85 per cent of patients have haemophilia A, most of the rest have haemophilia B.
117663.m: Haemophilia A is the most common form.

117664.q: How is bleeding in severe haemophilia usually prevented today?
117664.e: For prevention, factor concentrates are injected into a vein several times a week so that the factor level does not fall too low.
117664.m: Regular factor doses protect people with haemophilia from bleeding.

117665.q: Where does bleeding typically occur in severe haemophilia?
a: In the lens of the eye
117665.e: Repeated bleeding into joints (haemarthrosis), for example in the knee, can permanently damage the joints without treatment.
117665.m: Haemophilia typically leads to bleeding into the joints.

117666.q: Which European queen was a carrier of haemophilia, which spread into several royal houses?
117666.e: Through Queen Victoria's daughters, haemophilia reached the Russian imperial family, among others, where the heir to the throne Alexei had the disease.
117666.m: Queen Victoria spread haemophilia through Europe's royal houses.

117667.q: What is missing from the blood in haemophilia?
117667.e: In haemophilia A, clotting factor VIII is missing; in haemophilia B, factor IX. That is why it takes much longer for bleeding to stop.
117667.m: In haemophilia, a clotting factor is missing.

117668.q: Which new treatment aims to supply people with haemophilia with the missing clotting factor permanently?
117668.e: In gene therapy, a working copy of the gene is placed into liver cells. These cells then make the missing clotting factor themselves.
117668.m: Gene therapy lets the body make the missing clotting factor itself.

117669.q: Why does haemophilia affect almost only males?
a: The gene is on the X chromosome
The gene is on the Y chromosome
117669.e: Males have only one X chromosome. If the gene for the clotting factor on it is altered, there is no healthy backup gene. Females have two X chromosomes and are usually only carriers.
117669.m: Haemophilia is inherited on the X chromosome.

117670.q: Where does the anticoagulant heparin get its name from?
a: From the liver, from which it was first isolated
From the Latin word for blood
117670.e: In 1916 the medical student Jay McLean isolated an anticoagulant substance from dog liver; William Henry Howell named it after the Greek hepar, liver.
117670.m: Heparin is named after the liver.

117671.q: How do vitamin K antagonists such as Marcoumar work?
a: They block the production of clotting factors
They thin the blood with water
They lower the number of red blood cells
117671.e: The liver needs vitamin K to make several clotting factors. Vitamin K antagonists block this step, so the blood clots more slowly.
117671.m: Vitamin K antagonists slow down the production of clotting factors.

117672.q: Which heparins are usually injected under the skin once a day today to prevent thromboses?
117672.e: Low-molecular-weight heparins such as nadroparin or enoxaparin are almost fully absorbed under the skin and work for a long time; they are the treatment of choice for preventing thrombosis.
117672.m: Low-molecular-weight heparins are injected under the skin to prevent thrombosis.

117673.q: What are anticoagulants such as rivaroxaban often prescribed for?
a: Against blood clots, for example in atrial fibrillation
117673.e: In atrial fibrillation or after a thrombosis, clots can form that cause a stroke or a pulmonary embolism. Anticoagulants lower this risk.
117673.m: Anticoagulants protect against dangerous blood clots.

117674.q: Why do people often have to pause an anticoagulant before a planned operation?
a: So that the anaesthetic works better
Because otherwise it causes a fever
So that the wound itches sooner
117674.e: Anticoagulants slow down how fast bleeding stops. During an operation you could therefore lose a dangerous amount of blood.
117674.m: The biggest danger of anticoagulants is bleeding.

117675.q: What was the drug warfarin originally developed from?
a: From a substance in spoiled sweet clover
From the saliva of vampire bats
117675.e: In mouldy sweet clover, dicoumarol forms, which made cattle bleed to death; warfarin was developed from it, first as rat poison.
117675.m: Warfarin comes from a substance in spoiled sweet clover.

117676.q: Why do many blood collection tubes contain citrate or EDTA?
a: They bind calcium and so prevent clotting
They kill bacteria in the blood
They dissolve the red blood cells
117676.e: Without free calcium ions, the clotting cascade cannot run, so the sample stays liquid.
117676.m: Calcium binders keep blood samples liquid.

117677.q: Which antidote reverses the effect of vitamin K antagonists?
117677.e: Vitamin K antagonists block the vitamin K dependent production of clotting factors; added vitamin K reverses this effect within hours.
117677.m: Vitamin K is the antidote to vitamin K antagonists.

117678.q: For which disease is a bone marrow or stem cell transplant used especially often?
117678.e: In leukaemia, the bone marrow makes malignant blood cells. After strong chemotherapy, donated stem cells rebuild a healthy blood system. The pioneer of this method was E. Donnall Thomas, Nobel Prize 1990.
117678.m: Stem cell transplants help especially with leukaemia.

117679.q: Which tissue markers should match as closely as possible in an allogeneic stem cell transplant?
117679.e: HLA molecules decide whether immune cells recognise tissue as foreign; a good match lowers rejection and complications.
117679.m: For stem cell donations, the HLA markers must match.

117680.q: What is the complication called in which the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's body?
117680.e: T cells transferred with the graft recognise the recipient's tissue as foreign and can damage skin, gut and liver.
117680.m: In graft-versus-host disease, the donor's immune system attacks the recipient.

117681.q: What does an autologous stem cell transplant mean?
a: The patient gets their own stem cells back
The stem cells come from a sibling
The stem cells come from an animal
The stem cells come from a cell culture of other donors
117681.e: In an autologous transplant, the patient's own stem cells are collected before high-dose chemotherapy and given back afterwards.
117681.m: Autologous means the stem cells come from the patient themselves.

117682.q: How are blood stem cells for a transplant usually collected today?
117682.e: For a few days the donor receives a medicine (G-CSF) that draws stem cells from the bone marrow into the blood. A machine then collects them from the venous blood. Less often, bone marrow is taken from the hip bone.
117682.m: Stem cells are usually collected from venous blood today.

117683.q: How likely is it that a sibling has the same HLA markers?
117683.e: Each child inherits one of two HLA haplotypes from each parent; the same combination occurs with a probability of 1/2 · 1/2.
117683.m: Siblings are HLA-identical in 25 per cent of cases.

117684.q: Which desired effect can help against leukaemia in an allogeneic transplant?
117684.e: Donor immune cells can recognise remaining leukaemia cells as foreign and destroy them.
117684.m: Donor cells can fight remaining leukaemia cells.

117685.q: Which source of blood stem cells can be collected right after birth?
117685.e: Umbilical cord blood contains many blood stem cells and can be frozen and stored in cord blood banks.
117685.m: Umbilical cord blood is a source of blood stem cells.

117686.q: What requirements does Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland name for giving blood?
a: Healthy, at least 18 years old and weighing at least 50 kg
At least 16 years old and weighing at least 40 kg
At least 21 years old and weighing at least 60 kg
At least 25 years old, any weight
117686.e: According to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland, healthy people aged 18 or over who weigh at least 50 kg may donate (as of 2025).
117686.m: In Switzerland you may give blood from age 18 and 50 kg.

117687.q: How much blood is taken in Switzerland during a whole blood donation?
117687.e: According to Blood Transfusion SRC, 450 ml of blood is taken during a whole blood donation (as of 2025).
117687.m: In a whole blood donation you give 450 ml of blood.

117688.q: How long does a red blood cell concentrate keep, according to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland?
117688.e: Red blood cells can be stored chilled for up to 42 days (as of 2025).
117688.m: Red blood cell concentrates keep for up to 42 days.

117689.q: Why do platelet donations have to be replenished especially often?
a: They only keep for about 7 days
They may only be transported frozen
They only suit blood group AB
They are only needed in winter
117689.e: Platelet concentrates are stored at room temperature and, according to Blood Transfusion SRC, only keep for 7 days.
117689.m: Platelets only keep for about a week.

117690.q: How long can frozen blood plasma be stored, according to Blood Transfusion SRC Switzerland?
117690.e: Deep-frozen plasma can be stored for up to 24 months (as of 2025).
117690.m: Frozen plasma keeps for up to two years.

117691.q: Which blood group is the universal donor for blood plasma?
117691.e: Plasma of group AB contains neither anti-A nor anti-B antibodies and can therefore be given to all recipients.
117691.m: Plasma of blood group AB suits all recipients.

117693.q: What is the procedure called in which only plasma or platelets are taken and the other components are given back?
117693.e: In apheresis, a cell separator splits the blood and returns the components that are not needed straight back into the vein.
117693.m: In apheresis you get back the blood components that are not needed.

117694.q: Which value is checked before every blood donation to rule out anaemia in the donor?
117694.e: If haemoglobin is too low, the donor is deferred for their own protection.
117694.m: Haemoglobin is measured before a blood donation.

117695.q: Which cells in the bone marrow does erythropoietin mainly act on?
a: Precursor cells of red blood cells
117695.e: Erythropoietin binds to receptors on erythroid precursor cells, prevents them from dying and promotes their division and maturation.
117695.m: Erythropoietin supports the precursors of red blood cells.

117696.q: What happens in a pulmonary embolism?
a: A blood clot carried in the blood blocks a pulmonary artery
The lung fills with air from the abdomen
A lung collapses because of a tear
117696.e: Often a clot breaks loose from a leg vein and is carried with the blood into the lung. There it blocks an artery, and oxygen uptake is disturbed.
117696.m: In a pulmonary embolism, a clot blocks a pulmonary artery.

117697.q: Which well-known painkiller should people with haemophilia avoid?
117697.e: Acetylsalicylic acid inhibits the platelets and so increases the tendency to bleed. Paracetamol, on the other hand, is considered a suitable painkiller in haemophilia.
117697.m: With a tendency to bleed, aspirin is off limits.

117993.q: What is the main job of surfactant in the air sacs of the lungs?
a: It carries oxygen into the blood
117993.e: Surfactant is a film at the boundary between air and fluid in the alveoli. It reduces surface tension and so stops the air sacs from collapsing when you breathe out.
117993.m: Surfactant keeps the air sacs open by lowering surface tension.

117994.q: What everyday thing is the effect of surfactant best compared with?
a: Washing-up liquid, which lowers the surface tension of water
117994.e: Like washing-up liquid, surfactant reduces surface tension. This makes the air sacs easier to open and stops them from collapsing.
117994.m: Surfactant lowers surface tension like washing-up liquid.

117995.q: Which class of substances makes up most of surfactant?
117995.e: Surfactant consists of around 90 per cent lipids, mainly phospholipids, and about 10 per cent proteins.

117996.q: Without surfactant, what would happen to small air sacs when you breathe out?
117996.e: Surface tension pulls the moist inner wall of the air sacs together. Without surfactant, small air sacs in particular would collapse.

117997.q: Which condition typically arises in premature babies because of a lack of surfactant?
117997.e: The lungs of babies born very early still make too little surfactant. The alveoli collapse and respiratory distress syndrome (IRDS) develops.
117997.m: A lack of surfactant causes respiratory distress syndrome in premature babies.

117998.q: Why is breathing so tiring for premature babies who lack surfactant?
a: The air sacs have to be opened again with every breath
They only breathe through their skin
117998.e: Without surfactant, the air sacs collapse when breathing out. Every breath in takes a lot of strength to open them again.
117998.m: A lack of surfactant makes every breath a big effort.

117999.q: According to Laplace's law, how does the pressure in an air sac depend on its radius if surface tension stays the same?
a: It is inversely proportional to the radius
It is proportional to the radius
It grows with the square of the radius
It does not depend on the radius
117999.e: According to Laplace, P equals 2 times surface tension divided by radius. Without surfactant, small alveoli would have a higher pressure and would empty into large ones.
117999.m: The smaller a bubble, the higher its internal pressure.

118000.q: How is artificial surfactant given to premature babies?
a: As an injection into the muscle
As a drip into a vein
118000.e: Surfactant has to reach the alveoli. That is why it is given directly into the windpipe through a tube or a thin catheter.
118000.m: Surfactant is given to premature babies directly into the windpipe.

118001.q: In which part of the brain is the respiratory centre mainly located?
118001.e: The neurons that create the breathing rhythm lie in the medulla oblongata of the brainstem. The pons also plays a part.
118001.m: The respiratory centre is in the medulla oblongata.

118002.q: Which stimulus is the strongest drive to breathe in a healthy person?
118002.e: Even small rises in CO2 partial pressure increase breathing clearly. Lack of oxygen only becomes an important drive when the O2 partial pressure is very low.
118002.m: In healthy people, carbon dioxide is the main drive to breathe.

118003.q: What do the central chemoreceptors in the brainstem mainly react to?
a: A drop in pH in the cerebrospinal fluid
A lack of oxygen in the cerebrospinal fluid
A lack of glucose in the blood
118003.e: CO2 passes easily through the blood-brain barrier and lowers the pH of the cerebrospinal fluid. The central chemoreceptors detect this acidification.
118003.m: Central chemoreceptors measure the acidification of the cerebrospinal fluid.

118004.q: Where are the peripheral chemoreceptors that mainly report a lack of oxygen?
a: In the carotid and aortic bodies
In the kidneys and adrenal glands
In the air sacs of the lungs
In the atria of the heart
118004.e: The carotid body at the fork of the carotid artery and the aortic bodies on the aortic arch measure the O2 partial pressure of the blood.
118004.m: Carotid and aortic bodies report a lack of oxygen to the brain.

118005.q: What prevents the lungs from being overstretched when you breathe in deeply?
a: Stretch receptors in the lungs stop the breath in
The heart squeezes the lungs together
The ribs break easily when overstretched
118005.e: Stretch receptors in the lungs report strong filling to the respiratory centre via the vagus nerve. Breathing in is then stopped.
118005.m: Stretch receptors protect the lungs from overstretching.

118006.q: Which muscle does most of the work when you breathe in calmly?
118006.e: The diaphragm contracts and flattens. This enlarges the chest cavity, and air flows into the lungs.
118006.m: The diaphragm is the most important breathing muscle.

118007.q: Why is heavy hyperventilating before diving dangerous?
a: The urge to breathe comes too late
118007.e: Hyperventilation mainly lowers the CO2 level, but hardly increases the oxygen supply. The urge to breathe then comes so late that you can pass out under water (shallow water blackout).
118007.m: Hyperventilating before diving can make you pass out under water.

118008.q: Why do we keep breathing in our sleep without thinking about it?
a: The respiratory centre in the brainstem controls breathing automatically
The lungs move by themselves without nerves
The heart pumps the air into the lungs
The cerebrum takes over control at night
118008.e: Nerve cells in the brainstem constantly create a breathing rhythm. You can influence breathing consciously, but it also carries on without your will.

a: The total pressure is the sum of the partial pressures
A gas dissolves in proportion to temperature
Gases always diffuse towards higher pressure
118009.e: In a gas mixture, each gas contributes its share to the total pressure. These partial pressures add up to the total pressure.
118009.m: The partial pressures of all gases together make up the total pressure.

118010.q: Roughly what is the O2 partial pressure of dry air at sea level?
118010.e: Oxygen makes up about 21 per cent of air. 0.21 times 101.3 kPa gives about 21 kPa, or roughly 160 mmHg.
118010.m: At sea level, the O2 partial pressure of air is about 21 kPa.

118011.q: Why is the oxygen partial pressure in the air sacs lower than in the outside air?
a: The air there is mixed with water vapour and CO2
Oxygen is burned in the windpipe
The air pressure in the lungs is much higher
118011.e: In the alveoli, water vapour and exhaled CO2 are added, and oxygen is constantly taken up into the blood. That is why the O2 partial pressure is about 100 instead of 160 mmHg.
118011.m: There is less oxygen in the air sacs than in the outside air.

118012.q: What happens to the CO2 partial pressure in the blood when you breathe very fast and deeply (hyperventilate)?
118012.e: When you hyperventilate, you breathe out more CO2 than the body makes. The CO2 partial pressure falls below the normal value of about 40 mmHg, which can cause tingling and dizziness.
118012.m: Fast breathing lowers the CO2 level in the blood.

118013.q: Roughly what is the O2 partial pressure of dry air at an air pressure of 500 hPa (oxygen share 21 %)?
118013.e: The oxygen share stays the same at altitude. 0.21 times 500 hPa gives 105 hPa.
118013.m: The O2 partial pressure falls in the same proportion as the air pressure.

118014.q: What happens to inhaled air in the airways before it reaches the air sacs?
a: It is warmed and saturated with water vapour
118014.e: The mucous membranes warm the air to body temperature and moisten it completely. The water vapour then takes up part of the total pressure.
118014.m: The airways warm and moisten the air.

118015.q: What determines the direction of gas exchange between alveolus and blood?
a: The blood pressure in the aorta
118015.e: Gases always diffuse from where the partial pressure is higher to where it is lower. That is how oxygen gets into the blood and CO2 into the alveolus.
118015.m: Gases move from higher to lower partial pressure.

118016.q: According to Fick's law of diffusion, which change reduces gas exchange in the lungs?
118016.e: The rate of diffusion is proportional to surface area, diffusion coefficient and partial pressure difference, but inversely proportional to the thickness of the membrane.
118016.m: A thick membrane slows down gas exchange.

a: The amount of dissolved gas is proportional to the partial pressure
The volume of a gas is proportional to temperature
Pressure is inversely proportional to volume
Light gases diffuse faster than heavy ones
118017.e: According to Henry, the higher the partial pressure of a gas above a liquid, the more of it dissolves. This also applies to O2 and CO2 in blood plasma.
118017.m: The higher the partial pressure, the more gas dissolves in a liquid.

118018.q: What shape is the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin?
118018.e: The curve is sigmoid: in the middle range saturation rises steeply, at high partial pressures it levels off.
118018.m: The haemoglobin binding curve is S-shaped.

118019.q: What causes the typical shape of the curve for oxygen binding to haemoglobin?
a: The cooperative binding of the four subunits
The binding of iron to plasma proteins
The breakdown of haemoglobin in the spleen
118019.e: When one oxygen molecule binds to a subunit, the affinity of the others rises. This cooperativity creates the steep middle part of the curve.
118019.m: The four subunits of haemoglobin work together when binding.

118020.q: What is the advantage of the upper, flat part of the oxygen dissociation curve?
a: The blood stays almost fully saturated even when there is a little less oxygen in the air
The blood releases a lot of oxygen there
The heart has to pump less there
118020.e: In the flat part, saturation hardly changes when the oxygen pressure drops a little. That is why the blood is still well loaded even at moderate altitude.
118020.m: The flat part of the curve secures oxygen uptake in the lungs.

118021.q: Which change shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right?
a: A fall in CO2 partial pressure
118021.e: Warmth lowers the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen. That is why more oxygen is released in warm, working tissue.
118021.m: Warmth makes it easier to release oxygen to the tissue.

118022.q: How does the body adapt to the lack of oxygen during a longer stay at high altitude?
a: It makes more red blood cells
118022.e: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more EPO. The bone marrow produces more red blood cells, and the blood can carry more oxygen.
118022.m: At altitude the body makes more red blood cells.

118023.q: Where is the binding curve of fetal haemoglobin (HbF) compared with that of adult haemoglobin?
118023.e: HbF binds 2,3-BPG less well and therefore has a higher affinity for oxygen. This lets the fetus take over oxygen from the mother's blood.
118023.m: Fetal haemoglobin binds oxygen more strongly than adult haemoglobin.

118024.q: What shape is the oxygen binding curve of myoglobin?
118024.e: Myoglobin has only one haem group and does not bind cooperatively. Its curve is hyperbolic and lies far to the left, which makes it an oxygen store in muscle.
118024.m: Myoglobin has a hyperbolic binding curve.

118025.q: Roughly how much more strongly does haemoglobin bind carbon monoxide than oxygen?
118025.e: Carbon monoxide binds about 200 to 300 times more tightly to haemoglobin than oxygen does. Even low CO concentrations therefore block a lot of haemoglobin.
118025.m: Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen off haemoglobin very effectively.

118026.q: Roughly what is the oxygen saturation of arterial blood in a healthy person at sea level?
118026.e: At an O2 partial pressure of about 100 mmHg, the curve is in its flat upper part. Haemoglobin there is about 96 to 98 per cent saturated.
118026.m: In healthy people, arterial blood is almost fully saturated with oxygen.

118027.q: What does the Bohr effect describe?
a: Haemoglobin releases oxygen more easily as pH falls
Haemoglobin binds less oxygen in the cold
Carbon monoxide pushes oxygen off haemoglobin
118027.e: When CO2 partial pressure and proton concentration rise, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls. Oxygen is then released more easily.
118027.m: An acidic environment loosens the binding of oxygen to haemoglobin.

118028.q: Which scientist is the Bohr effect named after?
118028.e: The Danish physiologist Christian Bohr described the effect. He was the father of the physicist Niels Bohr.
118028.m: The Bohr effect comes from the physiologist Christian Bohr.

118029.q: Which substance is produced in working muscles, lowers the pH of the blood and so helps haemoglobin release oxygen?
118029.e: Working muscles produce a lot of carbon dioxide. In the blood it forms carbonic acid, the pH falls, and haemoglobin releases more oxygen.
118029.m: A lot of carbon dioxide in the tissue helps release oxygen.

118030.q: Where in the body is the Bohr effect especially useful?
118030.e: Working muscles produce a lot of CO2 and acid. As a result, haemoglobin releases more oxygen there, exactly where it is needed.
118030.m: Active muscles get more oxygen thanks to the Bohr effect.

118031.q: In what form is most carbon dioxide carried in the blood?
118031.e: In the red blood cells, CO2 reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which breaks down into hydrogen carbonate and protons. Only a small part of the CO2 is dissolved or bound to haemoglobin.
118031.m: Carbon dioxide mostly travels in the blood as hydrogen carbonate.

118032.q: How does the oxygen dissociation curve of haemoglobin shift when the blood becomes more acidic?
a: To the right, oxygen is released more easily
To the left, oxygen is bound more tightly
Not at all, pH has no effect
118032.e: In the Bohr effect, haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen falls. The curve shifts to the right, and at the same oxygen pressure more oxygen is released.
118032.m: Acidic blood shifts the oxygen dissociation curve to the right.

118033.q: What does the Bohr effect do in the lung capillaries, where CO2 is breathed out?
118033.e: When CO2 is breathed out, the pH of the blood in the lungs rises. Haemoglobin's affinity for O2 increases, and oxygen is bound more easily.
118033.m: In the lungs, the Bohr effect helps with oxygen uptake.

118034.q: What happens to the pH of the blood when you hyperventilate heavily and breathe out a lot of carbon dioxide?
118034.e: Carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid in the blood. When a lot of CO2 is breathed out, this acid is missing and the pH rises. This is called respiratory alkalosis.
118034.m: Hyperventilation makes the blood more alkaline.

118035.q: From roughly what altitude does acute mountain sickness typically occur?
118035.e: Acute mountain sickness usually occurs above about 2500 m, especially when climbing quickly without acclimatising.
118035.m: Above about 2500 m there is a risk of altitude sickness.

118036.q: Which symptom is the most typical key symptom of acute mountain sickness?
118036.e: Headache is the most important sign. Nausea, loss of appetite, tiredness, dizziness and poor sleep are often added.
118036.m: A headache at altitude is a warning sign.

118037.q: What is the life-threatening form called in which fluid builds up in the lungs at altitude?
118037.e: In high-altitude pulmonary oedema (HAPE), the high pressure in the lung vessels pushes fluid into the alveoli. Shortness of breath at rest and coughing are typical.
118037.m: Shortness of breath at rest at high altitude can mean pulmonary oedema.

118038.q: Which form of altitude sickness shows itself through unsteady walking and confusion?
118038.e: In high-altitude cerebral oedema (HACE), the brain swells. Unsteady walking (ataxia), confusion and reduced consciousness are alarm signs.
118038.m: Confusion at high altitude is an emergency.

118039.q: What is the most important measure in severe altitude sickness?
a: Taking a longer rest where you are
118039.e: Going down a few hundred metres quickly improves the oxygen supply. Medicines or hyperbaric bags only bridge the time until descent is possible.
118039.m: In severe altitude sickness you must descend immediately.

118040.q: What is the most effective way to prevent acute mountain sickness?
a: A slow ascent with rest days
A fast ascent, to spend little time at the top
Lots of coffee before the ascent
A day of fasting before the tour
118040.e: The body needs time to adapt to the lower oxygen pressure. Medicines such as acetazolamide can also help, but they do not replace a slow ascent.
118040.m: Climbing slowly is the best way to prevent altitude sickness.

118041.q: Why does faster, deeper breathing help the body adapt to high altitude?
a: It brings more oxygen into the lungs
It slows the production of red blood cells
118041.e: At altitude the oxygen pressure of the air is lower. If you breathe more, more oxygen reaches the air sacs. Medicines such as acetazolamide encourage this increased breathing.
118041.m: At altitude, breathing more brings more oxygen into the blood.

118042.q: Above 3000 m, by how much at most should your sleeping altitude rise per day?
118042.e: Common recommendations advise raising your sleeping altitude above 3000 m by no more than 300 to 500 m per day. That gives the body time to adapt.
118042.m: Above 3000 m, raise your sleeping altitude only slowly.

118043.q: Why does a portable hyperbaric bag help in severe altitude sickness?
118043.e: In the inflated bag, the air pressure rises. For the body it is as if it were a few hundred to over a thousand metres lower. This bridges the time until descent.
118043.m: A hyperbaric bag artificially brings the body to a lower altitude.

118044.q: What is it called when the body's tissue gets too little oxygen?
118044.e: Hypoxia means a lack of oxygen in the tissue. Hyperthermia is overheating, hypotension is low blood pressure and hyperglycaemia is blood sugar that is too high.
118044.m: Hypoxia means a lack of oxygen in the tissue.

118045.q: Why can tissue lack oxygen after heavy blood loss, even though you are breathing normally?
a: There are not enough red blood cells to carry it
The lungs no longer take up oxygen
The blood contains too much oxygen
The muscles no longer use oxygen
118045.e: In the blood, oxygen is mainly bound to the haemoglobin of the red blood cells. If many of them are missing, the blood carries too little oxygen despite good breathing.
118045.m: Without enough haemoglobin, the blood lacks the capacity to carry oxygen.

118046.q: Why is cyanide poisoning so dangerous, even though there is enough oxygen in the blood?
a: The cells can no longer use the oxygen
The blood can no longer bind oxygen
The heart beats far too slowly
118046.e: Cyanide blocks an enzyme of cellular respiration in the mitochondria. The oxygen does reach the cells, but cannot be used there to produce energy.
118046.m: In cyanide poisoning, the cells cannot use oxygen.

118047.q: How can you recognise cyanosis when there is a serious lack of oxygen?
a: By red spots on the neck
118047.e: Oxygen-poor haemoglobin is darker than oxygen-rich haemoglobin. If there is a lot of it in the blood, the lips, skin and fingertips look bluish.
118047.m: Cyanosis shows as a blue colour of the skin and lips.

118048.q: Which device measures oxygen saturation on the finger without taking blood?
118048.e: The pulse oximeter shines red and infrared light through the finger. From the different absorption it calculates the saturation.
118048.m: The pulse oximeter measures saturation with light.

118049.q: How does the body adapt to the lack of oxygen after a few weeks at high altitude?
a: It makes more red blood cells
It makes fewer red blood cells
118049.e: When oxygen is short, cells switch on protective programmes, including one for the hormone EPO. As a result, the number of red blood cells rises and the blood can carry more oxygen.
118049.m: At altitude the body makes more red blood cells.

118050.q: Which hormone does the kidney produce more of when oxygen is short?
118050.e: Erythropoietin (EPO) stimulates the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow. This increases the capacity to carry oxygen.
118050.m: When oxygen is short, the kidney makes more erythropoietin.

118051.q: The lungs divert blood from poorly ventilated areas to well ventilated ones. What is the purpose of this?
a: So that as much blood as possible can take up oxygen
So that the lungs need less energy
So that the heart beats more slowly
So that more carbon dioxide stays in the blood
118051.e: Blood flowing through poorly ventilated areas of the lungs hardly takes up any oxygen. That is why the vessels there narrow, and the blood flows to the well ventilated air sacs.
118051.m: Lung vessels narrow where there is a local lack of oxygen.

118052.q: Roughly how large is the anatomical dead space of an adult?
118052.e: In adults the anatomical dead space is about 150 ml. This air does not reach the alveoli.
118052.m: The anatomical dead space holds about 150 millilitres.

118053.q: What is part of the anatomical dead space?
118053.e: The nose, throat, windpipe, bronchi and bronchioles only conduct air. No gas exchange takes place in them.
118053.m: No gas exchange takes place in the conducting airways.

118054.q: What are ventilated alveoli called that receive no blood flow?
118054.e: If alveoli are ventilated but receive no blood, for example in a pulmonary embolism, they take no part in gas exchange. They form the alveolar dead space.
118054.m: Ventilated alveoli without blood flow are alveolar dead space.

118055.q: What does the physiological (functional) dead space consist of?
118055.e: The physiological dead space is the sum of all volumes without gas exchange. In healthy people it is almost the same as the anatomical dead space.
118055.m: The physiological dead space includes anatomical and alveolar dead space.

118056.q: Roughly what share of a normal 500 ml breath does not reach the alveoli?
118056.e: With a 500 ml breath, about 150 ml stays in the conducting airways. That is about a third; only the rest takes part in gas exchange.
118056.m: About a third of a normal breath stays in the dead space.

118057.q: Why is shallow, fast breathing not very effective?
a: A large part of each breath stays in the dead space
The alveoli are destroyed by it
118057.e: With small breaths, the dead space stays the same size but makes up a larger share. Little fresh air is left for the alveoli.
118057.m: Deep breaths are more effective than shallow ones.

118058.q: What does a very long snorkel do when diving?
118058.e: The tube is extra dead space. Exhaled, CO2-rich air is breathed in again, and fresh air reaches the alveoli less well.
118058.m: A snorkel extends the dead space.

118059.q: Why does a pulmonary embolism enlarge the dead space?
a: Ventilated alveoli no longer receive blood
The lungs are no longer ventilated
118059.e: In a pulmonary embolism, a clot blocks a pulmonary artery. The affected alveoli are still ventilated but no longer receive blood, and take no part in gas exchange.
118059.m: A pulmonary embolism creates ventilated alveoli without blood flow.

118060.q: What does vital capacity tell you?
a: The maximum volume you can breathe out after breathing in as far as possible
The volume of a normal breath at rest
The volume that stays in the lungs after breathing out
The amount of air per minute when breathing at rest
118060.e: Vital capacity is the sum of the inspiratory reserve volume, tidal volume and expiratory reserve volume.
118060.m: Vital capacity is the largest movable lung volume.

118061.q: Which lung volume cannot be measured with a simple spirometer?
118061.e: The residual volume stays in the lungs even after breathing out as far as possible. Because it is never breathed out, the spirometer cannot record it.
118061.m: The residual volume always stays in the lungs.

118062.q: What is the volume called that is breathed out in the first second of a forced breath out?
a: Forced expiratory volume in one second
118062.e: The forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1) measures how much air you can breathe out forcefully in one second after a deep breath in. It falls when the airways are narrowed.
118062.m: FEV1 shows how fast you can breathe air out.

118063.q: Which spirometry value falls during an asthma attack because the airways are narrowed?
a: The amount of air you can breathe out in one second
118063.e: Air flows more slowly through narrowed bronchi. That is why you can forcefully breathe out less air in the first second.
118063.m: When the airways are narrowed, FEV1 falls.

118064.q: What is typically reduced in pulmonary fibrosis, where the lung tissue becomes stiff?
118064.e: Stiff lung tissue is hard to stretch. That is why you cannot breathe in as deeply and the vital capacity is smaller.
118064.m: A stiff lung has a smaller vital capacity.

118065.q: Roughly how large is an adult's tidal volume at rest?
118065.e: At rest, an adult moves about half a litre of air with each breath.
118065.m: A calm breath is about half a litre.

118066.q: Which simple device do people with asthma use at home to measure their maximum breathing-out flow?
118066.e: The peak flow meter measures the highest flow speed when you breathe out forcefully. Falling values show the airways are narrowing more.
118066.m: With a peak flow meter you check your airways at home.

118067.q: Why do you usually wear a nose clip during spirometry?
a: So that no air escapes through the nose
So that you do not sneeze
So that the nose does not dry out
So that you breathe in faster
118067.e: Only the air that flows through the mouthpiece is measured. If air escaped through the nose, the values would be wrong.
118067.m: During spirometry you breathe only through your mouth.

118068.q: Why do tall people usually have a higher vital capacity than short people?
a: They have a larger chest and larger lungs
They have more red blood cells
118068.e: Lung volumes depend strongly on body height. That is why measured values are always compared with reference values for age, sex and height.
118068.m: Vital capacity depends on body height.

118069.q: What is the most important cause of COPD in Switzerland and in industrialised countries worldwide?
118069.e: Smoking is the most important risk factor for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Stopping smoking is the most effective way to keep it from getting worse.
118069.m: Smoking is the main cause of COPD.

118070.q: Which test shows in COPD how much air you can breathe out and how fast?
118070.e: In spirometry you breathe out into a measuring device as hard as you can. In COPD, the amount of air in the first second is reduced compared with the total amount.
118070.m: COPD is detected with a lung function test.

118071.q: Which lung change with destroyed alveolar walls is often part of COPD?
118071.e: In emphysema, alveolar walls break down and large, floppy air sacs form. The exchange surface shrinks, and air gets trapped when breathing out.
118071.m: In emphysema the alveolar walls are destroyed.

118072.q: What does the word “obstructive” mean in the name COPD?
a: The lungs are inflamed and infectious
The lungs have grown too large
The respiratory centre in the brain is disturbed
118072.e: COPD stands for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Obstructive means that the airways are permanently narrowed and air escapes poorly when breathing out.
118072.m: In COPD the airways are permanently narrowed.

118073.q: Which three key symptoms are typical of COPD?
a: Breathlessness, skin rash, loss of appetite
118073.e: Typical of COPD are a chronic cough, sputum and breathlessness, at first during exertion. In German, the initials of these three words form the memory aid AHA.
118073.m: Cough, sputum and breathlessness are typical of COPD.

a: No, but its progress can be slowed
Yes, with a course of antibiotics
Yes, it heals by itself after a few weeks
118074.e: The damage to the bronchi and air sacs does not reverse. Stopping smoking, medicines and exercise training can, however, clearly slow down its progress.
118074.m: COPD cannot be cured, but its course can be slowed.

118075.q: Why do people with severe emphysema take up oxygen less well?
a: The exchange surface of the air sacs is smaller
Their blood no longer contains haemoglobin
118075.e: In emphysema, many small air sacs merge into large bubbles. This shrinks the surface through which oxygen enters the blood.
118075.m: Emphysema reduces the exchange surface of the lungs.

118076.q: Which breathing technique helps people with COPD stop the bronchi from collapsing when breathing out?
118076.e: In pursed-lip breathing, you breathe out against slightly closed lips. The back pressure keeps the floppy small airways open.
118076.m: Pursed-lip breathing keeps the airways open when breathing out.

118077.q: What happens in the lung tissue in pulmonary fibrosis?
a: Air bubbles form in the pleura
118077.e: In pulmonary fibrosis, the framework of the lungs scars. The tissue becomes stiff and gas exchange gets worse.
118077.m: In pulmonary fibrosis the lungs scar.

118078.q: What can today's medicines achieve against idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?
118078.e: Antifibrotic drugs such as pirfenidone and nintedanib slow down the scarring, but cannot cure it. In severe cases, a lung transplant remains an option.
118078.m: Medicines slow pulmonary fibrosis but do not cure it.

118079.q: Which pulmonary fibrosis is caused by breathing in asbestos fibres?
118079.e: Inhaled asbestos fibres cause scarring of the lungs, called asbestosis. In Switzerland asbestos has been banned since 1990.
118079.m: Asbestos fibres can make the lungs scar.

118080.q: Which dust causes silicosis, a typical occupational disease of miners?
118080.e: Silicosis is caused by breathing in crystalline silicon dioxide (quartz), for example in tunnel building or in quarries.

118081.q: Why do people with pulmonary fibrosis find it especially hard to breathe in deeply?
a: The scarred lung tissue is stiff
The bronchi are blocked with mucus
The lungs are overinflated with air
118081.e: Scar tissue stretches poorly, so the lungs expand less well. When listening with a stethoscope, you often hear fine crackles at the end of breathing in.
118081.m: A scarred lung is stiff and hard to stretch.

118082.q: Which measured value is typically reduced in pulmonary fibrosis because the exchange membrane is thickened?
118082.e: The diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) measures how well gas passes through the alveolar wall. It falls when the tissue is thickened.
118082.m: In pulmonary fibrosis the diffusing capacity falls.

118083.q: Which examination shows the scarring pattern of pulmonary fibrosis best?
a: A CT scan of the lungs
118083.e: In high-resolution CT, advanced fibrosis shows small cysts that look like a honeycomb.
118083.m: A CT scan shows the scars of pulmonary fibrosis.

118084.q: Besides inhaled dust, what else can cause pulmonary fibrosis?
a: Certain medicines, for example against cancer
118084.e: Some drugs, for example the cancer medicine bleomycin, can damage lung tissue. Radiation and autoimmune diseases can also cause fibrosis.
118084.m: Medicines can also cause pulmonary fibrosis.

118085.q: What is the minute ventilation with a tidal volume of 0.5 l and 12 breaths per minute?
118085.e: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate. 0.5 l times 12 per minute gives 6 l/min.
118085.m: Minute ventilation is tidal volume times breathing rate.

118086.q: What is the alveolar ventilation with a tidal volume of 500 ml, a dead space of 150 ml and 14 breaths per minute?
118086.e: With each breath, 500 ml minus 150 ml, so 350 ml, reaches the alveoli. 350 ml times 14 gives 4900 ml, or 4.9 l/min.
118086.m: Alveolar ventilation only counts the air beyond the dead space.

118087.q: Which acid-base disorder is caused by hyperventilation?
118087.e: When you hyperventilate, too much CO2 is breathed out. The CO2 partial pressure falls, and the pH of the blood rises.
118087.m: Hyperventilation makes the blood more alkaline.

118088.q: What happens to the CO2 in the blood if someone breathes too shallowly and too slowly for a long time?
a: It builds up, and the blood becomes more acidic
It decreases, and the blood becomes more alkaline
It stays the same, only the oxygen falls
It decreases, and the blood becomes more acidic
118088.e: If too little is breathed out, CO2 stays in the blood. This forms carbonic acid, and the pH of the blood falls.
118088.m: If you breathe too little, CO2 builds up and the blood becomes more acidic.

118089.q: Roughly how much air does an adult breathe in and out per minute at rest?
118089.e: At rest, each breath is about 0.5 litres, with around 12 to 16 breaths per minute. That gives about 6 to 8 litres per minute.
118089.m: At rest you breathe about 6 to 8 litres of air per minute.

118090.q: Where in the lungs does gas exchange between the air and the blood take place?
118090.e: The air sacs have very thin walls and are surrounded by fine capillaries. There the gases pass back and forth between air and blood.
118090.m: Gas exchange happens in the air sacs.

118091.q: What happens during gas exchange in the air sacs?
a: Oxygen goes into the blood, CO2 into the air
CO2 goes into the blood, oxygen into the air
Nitrogen goes into the blood, oxygen stays in the air
Water goes into the blood, CO2 stays in the blood
118091.e: By diffusion, each gas moves to where its concentration is lower. That is how oxygen gets into the blood and CO2 into the air you breathe out.
118091.m: In the air sacs, oxygen and CO2 swap places by diffusion.

118092.q: Which device takes over breathing in intensive care when someone can no longer breathe enough on their own?
118092.e: A ventilator blows air with oxygen into the lungs. A defibrillator gives electric shocks to the heart, a dialysis machine replaces the kidney.
118092.m: A ventilator helps when your own breathing is not enough.

118387.q: Which enzyme already starts splitting starch in the mouth?
118387.e: The salivary glands release alpha-amylase into saliva. It already splits starch into shorter pieces while you chew.
118387.m: Starch digestion already starts in the mouth.

118388.q: Which bonds in starch does alpha-amylase split?
118388.e: Alpha-amylase hydrolyses the alpha-1,4 links between glucose units inside the starch chains. Humans cannot split beta-1,4 bonds such as those in cellulose.
118388.m: Alpha-amylase breaks the alpha-1,4 bonds of starch.

118389.q: Which disaccharide is mainly produced when amylase splits starch?
118389.e: Amylase breaks starch down mainly into maltose, maltotriose and limit dextrins. Maltose consists of two glucose units.
118389.m: Amylase turns starch mainly into maltose.

118390.q: Why does bread taste slightly sweet when you chew it for a long time?
a: Amylase in saliva splits starch into sugar
Saliva itself contains a lot of sugar
The tongue makes sweeteners while chewing
The bread releases fat while being chewed
118390.e: Salivary amylase breaks the long starch chains in bread down into smaller sugars such as maltose. These taste sweet.
118390.m: Salivary amylase turns starch into sweet sugar.

118391.q: Besides the salivary glands, which organ also produces alpha-amylase for digestion?
118391.e: The pancreas releases pancreatic amylase into the duodenum. There it continues the digestion of starch.

118392.q: Why does salivary amylase soon stop working in the stomach?
118392.e: Salivary amylase works best at a neutral pH. As soon as stomach acid soaks through the food mass, the enzyme is inactivated.

118393.q: A greatly raised amylase level in the blood is a typical sign of which disease?
118393.e: When the pancreas is inflamed, more of its enzymes get into the blood. That is why amylase is measured in diagnosis.
