118393.m: High amylase in the blood can point to pancreatitis.

118394.q: Why does amylase no longer split starch after being heated to 100 °C?
a: The enzyme is denatured by the heat
The amylase is broken down into sugar
118394.e: Enzymes are proteins with a precise three-dimensional shape. Great heat destroys this shape, and the active site no longer fits the starch.
118394.m: Too much heat destroys enzymes such as amylase.

118395.q: You mix starch solution with saliva and test it repeatedly with iodine solution. What does it show when the blue colour disappears?
a: The starch has been broken down
118395.e: Iodine only turns long starch chains blue. If amylase splits the starch, the blue colour no longer appears.
118395.m: The iodine test shows whether starch is still present.

118396.q: In which inactive precursor form is pepsin produced?
118396.e: The stomach lining releases pepsin as pepsinogen. Only in the inside of the stomach is the active enzyme formed from it.

118397.q: Which substance in the stomach creates the acidic environment in which pepsin works?
118397.e: The stomach lining releases hydrochloric acid. It activates pepsinogen to pepsin and kills many germs in food.
118397.m: Hydrochloric acid makes the stomach acidic.

118398.q: What activates pepsinogen in the stomach?
a: Hydrochloric acid and pepsin that is already active
118398.e: In the acidic environment, a piece breaks off pepsinogen. Pepsin that has already formed speeds up this activation autocatalytically.
118398.m: Acid and pepsin itself activate pepsinogen.

118399.q: In which pH range does pepsin work best?
118399.e: Pepsin is adapted to the strongly acidic environment of the stomach. Its optimum is at a pH of about 1.5 to 2.

118400.q: In what form do the chief cells of the stomach first release pepsin?
a: As part of the hydrochloric acid
118400.e: Pepsin is released as the inactive precursor pepsinogen. Only stomach acid turns it into active pepsin, so the cells do not digest themselves.
118400.m: Pepsin forms in the stomach from the precursor pepsinogen.

118401.e: Pepsin splits proteins in the stomach into shorter polypeptides. Enzymes in the small intestine take over the further breakdown.

118402.q: What protects the stomach wall from being digested by pepsin itself?
118402.e: Mucous neck cells and the surface lining form a thick layer of mucus. It keeps acid and pepsin away from the lining cells.
118402.m: Mucus protects the stomach from digesting itself.

118403.q: What happens to pepsin when the food mass reaches the small intestine?
a: It stops working in the less acidic environment
It is absorbed into the blood and keeps working
118403.e: In the small intestine, the food mass is neutralised with bicarbonate. Pepsin needs a strongly acidic environment and loses its effect there; other enzymes take over.
118403.m: Pepsin only works in the acidic stomach.

118404.q: Where is the inactive precursor trypsinogen converted into active trypsin?
118404.e: An enzyme of the small intestine lining, enteropeptidase, cuts a short piece off trypsinogen in the duodenum. Only then is trypsin active.
118404.m: Trypsin is only activated in the small intestine.

118405.q: Which nutrients does the digestive enzyme trypsin split?
118405.e: Trypsin is a protease from the pancreas. It breaks down proteins in the small intestine into shorter peptides.
118405.m: Trypsin is a protein-splitting digestive enzyme.

118406.q: Why is trypsin also used in the lab to study proteins?
a: It cuts proteins only at very specific points
It stains proteins so they are visible
It builds proteins from amino acids
118406.e: Trypsin cuts after the amino acids lysine and arginine. Because the pieces are therefore predictable, it is often used in research.
118406.m: Trypsin cuts proteins at precisely defined points.

118407.q: Which enzyme precursor is activated directly by trypsin in the small intestine?
118407.e: Trypsin activates other pancreatic proenzymes such as chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidases. In this way it triggers an activation cascade.

118408.q: Why does the pancreas produce trypsin as an inactive precursor?
a: To protect itself from digesting itself
Because otherwise it would get into the blood
So that it can split fat
118408.e: Active trypsin would attack the tissue of the pancreas. It is only activated in the gut.
118408.m: Proenzymes protect the pancreas from digesting itself.

118409.q: At roughly what pH does trypsin work best?
118409.e: Trypsin works in the slightly alkaline environment of the small intestine. Its optimum is roughly at pH 8.
118409.m: Trypsin works in the slightly alkaline range.

118410.q: What can happen if trypsin already becomes active in the pancreas?
118410.e: Active trypsin attacks the body's own tissue and activates other enzymes. Normally the inhibitor SPINK1 blocks small amounts; if this protection fails, pancreatitis can develop.
118410.m: Trypsin that is active too early can attack the pancreas itself.

118411.q: In which inherited disease do too few digestive enzymes such as trypsin often get from the pancreas into the gut?
118411.e: In cystic fibrosis, thick mucus blocks the ducts of the pancreas. The enzymes do not reach the gut, so patients take enzyme capsules with their meals.
118411.m: In cystic fibrosis, digestive enzymes are often missing in the gut.

118412.q: Into which building blocks do lipases split dietary fats (triglycerides)?
a: Into fatty acids and glycerol parts
118412.e: A triglyceride consists of glycerol and three fatty acids. Pancreatic lipase usually splits off the two outer fatty acids, producing monoacylglycerol and free fatty acids.
118412.m: Lipases split fats into fatty acids and glycerol parts.

118413.q: Why do lipases in the gut need the help of bile salts?
a: Bile salts break the fat up into small droplets
Bile salts split the fat completely themselves
Bile salts make the fat acidic
Bile salts protect the fat from digestion
118413.e: Bile salts emulsify fat into fine droplets and so enlarge the surface on which lipase works. A helper protein, colipase, anchors the lipase to the droplet.
118413.m: Bile salts enlarge the fat surface for lipase.

118414.q: What kind of chemical bond do lipases split in a fat molecule?
118414.e: In fats, fatty acids are attached to glycerol by ester bonds. Lipases split these by adding water, preferably at the two outer positions.
118414.m: Lipases split the ester bonds of fats.

118415.q: Which lipase starts splitting fat even before the small intestine?
118415.e: The chief cells of the stomach make an acid-stable gastric lipase. It already splits a small part of the dietary fats.
118415.m: The stomach already splits some fat too.

118416.q: Which enzyme does the weight-loss medicine orlistat block in the gut?
118416.e: Orlistat blocks gastric and pancreatic lipases. Part of the dietary fat is then passed out undigested.
118416.m: Orlistat blocks fat splitting in the gut.

118417.q: Which class of enzymes do lipases belong to?
118417.e: Lipases split bonds by adding water. Like all digestive enzymes, they therefore belong to the hydrolases.

118418.q: What is a typical sign that too little pancreatic lipase is reaching the gut?
118418.e: Without enough lipase, fat is not split and not absorbed. The stools then become bulky, shiny and fatty (steatorrhoea).
118418.m: If lipase is missing, fatty stools result.

118419.q: Where does a lipase attack fats in the gut?
a: At the boundary between fat and water
118419.e: Lipases are water-soluble, their substrates are not. That is why they work on the surface of the fat droplets (interfacial activation).
118419.m: Lipase works on the surface of the fat droplets.

118420.q: From which starting material does the liver make bile acids?
118420.e: The liver converts cholesterol into bile acids in several enzyme steps. This is an important way of getting rid of cholesterol.
118420.m: Bile acids are made from cholesterol.

118421.e: The liver makes bile all the time. The gall bladder does not make it itself, it only stores and concentrates it.
118421.m: Bile is made in the liver, not in the gall bladder.

118422.q: How are secondary bile acids formed?
a: By being changed by gut bacteria
By being changed in the kidney
118422.e: Bacteria in the gut remove conjugates and hydroxyl groups from the primary bile acids. This produces, for example, deoxycholic acid and lithocholic acid.
118422.m: Gut bacteria turn primary bile acids into secondary ones.

118423.q: Bile acids in the gut help with the digestion of which nutrients?
118423.e: Bile acids break large drops of fat into fine droplets. This lets the fat-splitting enzymes work better.
118423.m: Bile acids help with fat digestion.

118424.q: What percentage of bile acids return to the liver through the enterohepatic circulation?
118424.e: Most bile acids are taken up again in the lower small intestine and carried back to the liver in the blood. Only a small remainder is lost in the stools.
118424.m: Almost all bile acids are reused.

118425.e: If bile contains too much cholesterol compared with bile acids, it comes out of solution and forms stones in the gall bladder.
118425.m: Most gallstones are made of cholesterol.

118426.q: Where does bile from the gall bladder go during a meal?
118426.e: After a fatty meal, the gall bladder contracts. Bile flows through the bile duct into the duodenum, the start of the small intestine.

118427.q: Where is bile stored and thickened between meals?
118427.e: The liver makes bile all the time. The gall bladder stores it and removes water from it, so it becomes more concentrated.
118427.m: The gall bladder stores and concentrates bile.

118428.q: What does the emulsification of dietary fats in the small intestine do?
a: Large fat drops break up into many small ones
118428.e: Bile salts and the mixing of the food mass break large fat drops into many fine droplets. No chemical bonds are split in the process.
118428.m: Emulsification enlarges the surface of fats.

118429.q: What does it mean that bile salts are amphiphilic?
a: They have water-loving and fat-loving parts
They are strongly acidic and alkaline
118429.e: Bile salts have a water-loving and a fat-loving side. This lets them sit at the boundary between fat and water.
118429.m: Amphiphilic substances link fat and water.

118430.q: What are the tiny clusters of bile salts and fat breakdown products that travel to the gut wall called?
118430.e: Bile salts form tiny micelles with monoacylglycerols and fatty acids. These carry the fat building blocks through the watery layer to the gut cell.
118430.m: Micelles carry fat building blocks to the gut wall.

118431.q: Which food is an emulsion of oil droplets in water?
118431.e: In mayonnaise, fine oil droplets are spread through the watery egg yolk and vinegar. Butter, the other way round, is an emulsion of water droplets in fat.

a: A fine mixture of two liquids that do not mix
A mixture of gas and liquid
118432.e: In an emulsion, droplets of one liquid are spread through another, for example oil in water. Milk is an example.
118432.m: An emulsion spreads one liquid finely through another.

118433.q: Besides bile salts, what helps emulsify fats mechanically?
a: The muscle movements of the stomach and gut
The breathing movements of the lungs
118433.e: The stomach and small intestine mix and knead the food mass hard. These shearing forces break up fat drops even further.
118433.m: Mixing the food mass helps with emulsifying.

118434.q: Which phospholipid in bile helps emulsify fats?
118434.e: Lecithin (phosphatidylcholine) is also amphiphilic. Together with the bile salts it forms mixed micelles.

118435.q: Why does emulsification speed up fat digestion even though it does not split any bonds?
a: The surface for enzymes to work on gets bigger
The fats are heated in the process
The enzymes are made in the process
118435.e: Fat-splitting enzymes can only work on the surface of the droplets. Many small droplets offer a much larger surface than one big drop.

118436.q: In which section of the digestive tract are most nutrients absorbed?
118436.e: The small intestine is long and, thanks to folds, villi and microvilli, has a huge surface. Most nutrients get into the blood there.
118436.m: The small intestine absorbs most nutrients.

118437.q: What are the tiny projections of the gut cell membrane that form the brush border called?
118437.e: Every gut lining cell carries thousands of microvilli on its surface. They greatly enlarge the absorbing surface once again.
118437.m: Microvilli form the brush border of gut cells.

118438.q: How does glucose get from the inside of the gut into the gut lining cell?
a: By secondary active transport together with sodium
118438.e: The transporter SGLT1 takes up glucose together with sodium ions. The energy comes from the sodium gradient maintained by the sodium-potassium pump.
118438.m: Glucose travels into the gut cell with sodium.

118439.q: Why do some people have trouble digesting milk sugar?
a: Their small intestine makes too little lactase
Their stomach makes too much acid
Their pancreas makes too little insulin
Their liver breaks down fat too slowly
118439.e: The enzyme lactase splits milk sugar into glucose and galactose, which are absorbed. If it is missing, the milk sugar reaches the large intestine and causes wind and stomach ache.
118439.m: Without lactase, milk sugar is not absorbed.

118440.q: Which factor from the parietal cells of the stomach is needed to absorb vitamin B12?
118440.e: Vitamin B12 binds to intrinsic factor and is only absorbed as a complex. If the factor is missing, pernicious anaemia can develop.
118440.m: Without intrinsic factor, no vitamin B12 is absorbed.

118441.q: After absorption in the small intestine, where do dietary fats go first before they reach the blood?
118441.e: In the gut cell, fats are packed into large fat droplets. These are too big for the blood vessels of the villi and take a detour through the lymph vessels before reaching the blood.
118441.m: Fats take a detour through the lymph.

118442.q: Which vitamins depend on micelles and fat digestion to be absorbed in the gut?
a: Vitamins A, D, E and K
Vitamins B1, B2, B6 and B12
118442.e: Vitamins A, D, E and K are fat-soluble. They are absorbed together with the products of fat breakdown, which is why poor fat digestion leads to a lack of them.
118442.m: Fat-soluble vitamins need fat to be absorbed.

118443.q: Which vessel first carries absorbed sugars and amino acids from the gut to the liver?
118443.e: The blood from the gut collects in the portal vein. This lets the liver process the absorbed substances first.
118443.m: The portal vein carries nutrients to the liver.

118444.q: In what form does the small intestine mainly absorb proteins from food?
a: As amino acids and short peptides
118444.e: Digestive enzymes break proteins down into amino acids and very short chains of two or three amino acids. Only these small building blocks can be taken up by the gut cells.
118444.m: Proteins are absorbed as small building blocks.

118445.q: In which section of the digestive tract do most bacteria live?
118445.e: Conditions in the large intestine are favourable and the food mass stays there a long time. Trillions of microorganisms live there.
118445.m: Most gut bacteria live in the large intestine.

118446.q: Which substances do gut bacteria mainly produce when breaking down dietary fibre?
118446.e: Bacteria ferment dietary fibre into acetate, propionate and butyrate. The body uses these short-chain fatty acids as energy and as signals.
118446.m: Bacteria turn dietary fibre into short-chain fatty acids.

118447.q: What effect can antibiotic treatment have on the gut flora?
a: Useful gut bacteria are killed as well
The gut flora is permanently strengthened
The gut bacteria become immune to viruses
It has no effect on the gut
118447.e: Antibiotics do not distinguish between harmful and useful bacteria. After treatment, the gut flora can therefore be changed for weeks, often with diarrhoea.
118447.m: Antibiotics also harm the useful gut flora.

118448.q: What is a disturbed balance in the make-up of the gut flora called?
118448.e: In dysbiosis, the variety of gut bacteria is reduced or shifted. It can occur, for example, after antibiotics.
118448.m: A disturbed gut flora is called dysbiosis.

118449.q: What do gut bacteria do for humans?
a: They make vitamin K, for example
They digest protein already in the mouth
118449.e: Gut bacteria make vitamins such as vitamin K and some B vitamins. They also break down dietary fibre and keep harmful germs in check.
118449.m: Gut bacteria supply us with vitamins such as vitamin K.

118450.q: What is transferred in a faecal transplant?
a: Gut bacteria from a healthy person
Stem cells from the bone marrow
A piece of healthy large intestine
118450.e: Prepared stool from a healthy donor brings a varied gut flora into the gut. It can push out harmful germs, for example after repeated infections caused by antibiotics.
118450.m: In a faecal transplant you receive healthy gut flora.

118451.q: What are indigestible food components called that specifically support useful gut bacteria?
118451.e: Prebiotics such as inulin serve as food for useful bacteria. Probiotics, on the other hand, are the living microorganisms themselves.
118451.m: Prebiotics feed the good gut bacteria.

118452.q: According to newer estimates, what is the ratio of bacterial cells to body cells in humans?
118452.e: The often quoted figure of 10 to 1 is considered outdated. An estimate from 2016 finds about as many bacteria as body cells.
118452.m: We carry about as many bacteria as our own cells.

118453.q: Which cells make the hormone gastrin?
118453.e: Gastrin comes mainly from the G cells in the antrum of the stomach. It is released into the blood.

118454.q: What is the most important effect of gastrin?
a: It increases hydrochloric acid production in the stomach
118454.e: Gastrin stimulates the parietal cells to produce acid. It also promotes the growth of the stomach lining.

118455.q: Which stimulus triggers the release of gastrin especially strongly?
a: Protein building blocks in the stomach
118455.e: Peptides and amino acids in the stomach and stretching of the stomach wall stimulate the G cells. The vagus nerve also promotes the release.
118455.m: Protein in the stomach triggers gastrin.

118456.q: Where in the body is the hormone gastrin mainly made?
118456.e: Gastrin is made in cells of the stomach lining in the lower part of the stomach. The name comes from the Greek word gaster, meaning stomach.

118457.q: How does gastrin get from the cells that make it to its target cells?
a: Through the lymph into the gut
118457.e: Gastrin is a hormone. Like all hormones, it is released into the blood and reaches the acid-producing cells in the stomach that way.
118457.m: Gastrin is spread through the blood like other hormones.

118458.q: What can be the result of producing too much stomach acid over a long time?
118458.e: Too much acid attacks the protective mucus layer of the stomach and the duodenum. Painful ulcers can develop.
118458.m: Too much stomach acid can cause ulcers.

118459.q: Which component of gastric juice is produced in greater amounts because of gastrin?
118459.e: Gastrin stimulates the parietal cells to produce hydrochloric acid. The acid kills germs and helps with protein digestion.
118459.m: Gastrin promotes the production of hydrochloric acid in the stomach.

118460.q: Where does the hormone gastrin get its name from?
a: From the Greek word for stomach
From the Latin word for gas
From the name of its discoverer
From the English word for hunger
118460.e: Gaster is Greek for stomach. The same word is found in gastritis, inflammation of the stomach lining.
118460.m: Gastrin is named after the stomach.

118461.q: Why does acidic gastric juice slow down the further release of gastrin?
a: It is negative feedback against too much acid
Acid destroys the cells that make it immediately
Acid dissolves the gastrin in the blood
118461.e: When there is enough acid in the stomach, less gastrin is released. That way the body regulates acid production itself, much like a thermostat controls the heating.
118461.m: A lot of stomach acid slows down gastrin release.

118462.q: Which hormone is considered the very first hormone ever discovered?
118462.e: William Bayliss and Ernest Starling detected it in 1902. They showed that a substance from the gut stimulates the pancreas through the blood.
118462.m: Secretin was the first hormone discovered.

118463.q: In which section of the digestive tract is secretin made?
118463.e: Secretin is made in the lining of the duodenum, just after the stomach. From there it enters the blood.
118463.m: Secretin is made in the duodenum.

118464.q: Which stimulus triggers the release of secretin?
a: Acidic food mass in the duodenum
118464.e: When acidic food mass reaches the duodenum and the pH there drops below about 4.5, secretin is released. That is how the gut reacts to stomach acid.
118464.m: Acid in the duodenum triggers secretin.

118465.q: What effect does secretin have on the pancreas?
118465.e: Secretin stimulates the duct cells of the pancreas to release fluid rich in bicarbonate. This neutralises stomach acid in the gut.
118465.m: Secretin brings bicarbonate from the pancreas.

118466.q: What effect does secretin have on the production of stomach acid?
118466.e: Secretin is released when too much acid arrives in the gut. It therefore slows acid production in the stomach and so protects the gut.

118467.q: What is the job of the bicarbonate that reaches the gut after a secretin signal?
118467.e: Bicarbonate is alkaline and raises the pH in the duodenum. This protects the gut lining and lets the digestive enzymes work.
118467.m: Bicarbonate from the pancreas neutralises stomach acid.

118468.q: Which group of hormones does secretin belong to?
118468.e: Secretin is a short chain of amino acids and therefore a peptide hormone. Steroid hormones such as cortisol, on the other hand, are built from cholesterol.

118469.q: How does secretin get from the gut to the pancreas?
118469.e: Like all hormones, secretin is released into the blood. Bayliss and Starling showed exactly that: the effect occurred even without a nerve connection.
118469.m: Hormones such as secretin travel in the blood.

118470.q: Which parts of the digestive tract can Crohn's disease affect?
a: The whole tract from mouth to anus
118470.e: Crohn's disease can affect any section of the digestive tract. Ulcerative colitis, on the other hand, is limited to the large intestine.
118470.m: Crohn's disease can occur anywhere in the digestive tract.

118471.q: How is the disease typically distributed in Crohn's disease?
a: In patches with healthy sections in between
Always in the whole gut at the same time
118471.e: Inflamed segments alternate with healthy sections (skip lesions). This distinguishes Crohn's from ulcerative colitis, which is continuous.
118471.m: Crohn's disease affects the gut in patches.

118472.q: How deep into the gut wall does the inflammation reach in Crohn's disease?
a: Through all layers of the wall
Only into the top layer of the lining
118472.e: The inflammation is transmural and affects all layers of the gut wall. As a result, fistulas and abscesses can form.
118472.m: Crohn's disease inflames the whole gut wall.

118473.q: Together with ulcerative colitis, which group of diseases does Crohn's disease belong to?
118473.e: Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the two most important chronic inflammatory bowel diseases. They usually come in flare-ups and are not contagious.
118473.m: Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease.

118474.q: Which complaints are typical of Crohn's disease?
118474.e: The inflammation in the gut causes cramping stomach pain and diarrhoea. Tiredness and weight loss are often added.
118474.m: Crohn's disease often shows as stomach pain and diarrhoea.

118475.q: Which lifestyle factor clearly increases the risk and severity of Crohn's disease?
118475.e: Smokers get the disease more often and have more severe courses. Stopping smoking is therefore part of the treatment.

118476.q: According to current knowledge, what works together in causing Crohn's disease?
a: Genes, the immune system and gut bacteria
118476.e: Certain gene variants, for example in the NOD2 gene, make people more susceptible. Together with environmental factors such as smoking, the immune system then overreacts to the gut bacteria.
118476.m: In Crohn's disease, genes, the immune system and the environment work together.

118477.q: Which typical complication arises in Crohn's disease because of the deep inflammation?
118477.e: The inflammation can bore through the wall and form channels to other organs or to the skin. Such fistulas often occur around the anus.
118477.m: Fistulas are a typical complication of Crohn's.

118478.q: Who is Crohn's disease named after?
118478.e: The American gastroenterologist Burrill B. Crohn described the disease with colleagues in 1932. Since then it has carried his name.
118478.m: Crohn's disease is named after Burrill B. Crohn.

118479.q: Which discovery earned Barry Marshall and Robin Warren the Nobel Prize in Medicine in 2005?
a: A bacterium causes many stomach ulcers
Stomach ulcers are caused only by stress
Stomach acid reliably kills all bacteria
118479.e: The two Australians showed that Helicobacter pylori causes inflammation of the stomach lining and ulcers. Before that, stress and acid were mainly thought to be the cause.
118479.m: Helicobacter pylori is a main cause of stomach ulcers.

118480.q: How does Helicobacter pylori survive in the very acidic environment of the stomach?
a: It neutralises the acid in its immediate surroundings
It lives only outside the stomach
It forms a shell of lime
118480.e: The bacterium makes an enzyme that produces ammonia from urea. Ammonia neutralises the acid around the bacterium.
118480.m: Helicobacter pylori protects itself by neutralising the acid around it.

118481.q: How can an infection with Helicobacter pylori be detected without a gastroscopy?
118481.e: You drink a solution containing labelled urea. If the bacterium is in the stomach, it splits the urea, and labelled carbon dioxide appears in your breath.
118481.m: A breath test reveals Helicobacter pylori.

118482.q: Which serious later disease can a years-long infection with Helicobacter pylori make more likely?
118482.e: The chronic inflammation damages the stomach lining over years. This clearly increases the risk of stomach cancer.
118482.m: A long-term infection with Helicobacter pylori increases the risk of stomach cancer.

118483.q: What shape is the bacterium Helicobacter pylori?
118483.e: The name “Helico” suggests a screw or spiral. With its shape and its flagella, the bacterium bores its way through the stomach mucus.
118483.m: Helicobacter pylori is a spiral-shaped bacterium.

118484.q: When do most people become infected with Helicobacter pylori?
a: Often in childhood, usually within the family
Only in old age in hospital
Only through mosquito bites in the tropics
118484.e: The bacterium is passed from person to person, often in childhood. Many infected people notice nothing for years.
118484.m: Helicobacter pylori is often passed on in childhood.

118485.q: What does the classic eradication therapy against Helicobacter pylori consist of?
a: An acid blocker plus two antibiotics
118485.e: A proton pump inhibitor is combined with two antibiotics, usually for 7 to 14 days. Because of resistance, four-drug therapies are often used today.
118485.m: Helicobacter pylori needs a combination therapy.

118486.q: How did Barry Marshall prove in 1984 that Helicobacter pylori causes stomach inflammation?
a: He drank a bacterial culture himself
118486.e: Marshall swallowed a culture of the bacterium and developed gastritis. The experiment on himself helped convince other experts.
118486.m: Barry Marshall proved his idea by experimenting on himself.

118786.q: Which enzyme links glucose units with α-1,4-glycosidic bonds during glycogenesis?
118786.e: Glycogen synthase attaches glucose units to the non-reducing end of a glycogen chain. It is the key enzyme of glycogen building.
118786.m: Glycogen synthase is the key enzyme of glycogenesis.

118788.q: Which hormone most strongly promotes glycogenesis in the liver and muscle?
118788.e: Insulin is released after a meal and activates glycogen synthase. That way extra glucose is stored.
118788.m: Insulin promotes the storage of glucose as glycogen.

118789.q: Which plant storage substance is similar to glycogen?
118789.e: Starch and glycogen both consist of glucose units and serve as stores. Cellulose is also made of glucose, but it is a structural material.
118789.m: Plants store sugar as starch, animals as glycogen.

118790.q: Why is the highly branched structure of glycogen useful?
a: Glucose can be broken off at many ends at the same time
It lets the cell save water
118790.e: Every branch creates an extra chain end. Enzymes can split off glucose at many ends at once, so the energy is available quickly.
118790.m: Many branches make glycogen quick to break down.

118791.q: Roughly how much glycogen does an adult's liver store?
118791.e: The liver stores about 100 grams of glycogen. Without food, this supply lasts only about a day.
118791.m: The liver stores only about 100 grams of glycogen.

118792.q: Which hormone makes glycogen break down quickly in stressful situations?
118792.e: Adrenaline prepares the body for fight or flight. It makes glycogen in the liver and muscles break down so that glucose is quickly available.
118792.m: Adrenaline releases glucose from glycogen during stress.

118793.q: In which two tissues do humans store the largest amounts of glycogen?
118793.e: The liver stores glycogen for the blood sugar of the whole body. Because of its large mass, skeletal muscle has the largest total glycogen store.
118793.m: Liver and muscles are the big glycogen stores.

118794.q: When does the body build up especially large amounts of glycogen?
a: After a meal rich in carbohydrates
118794.e: After a meal with lots of carbohydrates, blood sugar rises. Insulin then makes sure the liver and muscles store extra glucose as glycogen.
118794.m: After eating, the glycogen stores fill up.

118795.q: From which starting materials can the liver make glucose during gluconeogenesis?
a: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids
Acetyl-CoA, ketone bodies and fatty acids
118795.e: Lactate, glycerol from fat breakdown and glucogenic amino acids can be converted into pyruvate or intermediates of the citric acid cycle. From these, the liver builds new glucose.
118795.m: Lactate, glycerol and glucogenic amino acids are building blocks of gluconeogenesis.

a: Making new glucose from other substances
Taking up glucose in the gut
118796.e: In gluconeogenesis, the body builds new glucose from substances such as lactate, glycerol or amino acids. The name literally means making new sugar.

118797.q: In which organ does gluconeogenesis mainly take place?
118797.e: It is mainly the liver that makes new glucose and releases it into the blood. During long fasting, the kidney also contributes a share.
118797.m: The liver is the main site of gluconeogenesis.

a: During sugar digestion in the gut
118798.e: When nothing has been eaten for a long time and the glycogen stores run empty, the liver makes new glucose. That keeps blood sugar stable.
118798.m: During fasting the liver makes new glucose.

118799.q: Why is gluconeogenesis during fasting especially important for the brain?
a: The brain constantly needs glucose as a source of energy
The brain stores a lot of glycogen
The brain only breaks down protein
The brain does not need oxygen
118799.e: The brain can hardly store energy and depends on a continuous supply of glucose. Gluconeogenesis in the liver secures this supply.

118800.q: Which substance from hard-working muscles is built back into glucose in the liver?
118800.e: During intense exercise, muscles produce lactate. It travels in the blood to the liver, where it is converted back into glucose.
118800.m: The liver turns lactate back into glucose.

118801.q: Which hormone stimulates gluconeogenesis in the liver especially strongly?
118801.e: Glucagon is released from the alpha cells of the pancreas when blood sugar is low. In the liver it increases glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis.

118802.q: Is gluconeogenesis simply glycolysis in reverse?
a: No, some steps use different enzymes
Yes, all steps are exactly the same
No, it only takes place in plants
118802.e: Most steps are reversible, but three steps of glycolysis are not. Gluconeogenesis bypasses these with its own enzymes.
118802.m: Gluconeogenesis is not simply glycolysis in reverse.

a: It uses energy in the form of ATP
It produces a lot of ATP
It runs without any energy change
118803.e: Building glucose costs a lot of energy. The liver uses ATP and GTP for it, which it gets partly from breaking down fat.

118804.q: In which organ does the urea cycle mainly take place in humans?
118804.e: Only liver cells have all the enzymes of the urea cycle. The kidney then excretes the urea that has been made.
118804.m: Urea is made in the liver.

118805.q: Why does the body turn ammonia into urea?
a: Urea provides a lot of energy
Ammonia is too heavy for the blood
Urea is needed to build muscle
118805.e: Breaking down proteins produces poisonous ammonia. The liver turns it into harmless urea, which the kidneys excrete.
118805.m: Urea is the harmless form of ammonia.

118806.q: From which nutrients does the nitrogen excreted in urea come?
118806.e: Only proteins and their amino acids contain significant amounts of nitrogen. When the amino acids are broken down, it is excreted as urea.
118806.m: The nitrogen in urea comes from proteins.

118807.q: How does urea production change with a very high-protein diet?
118807.e: More protein means more broken-down amino acids and therefore more ammonia. The liver makes correspondingly more urea.
118807.m: A lot of protein leads to a lot of urea.

118808.q: What can happen when a badly damaged liver hardly makes any urea?
a: Ammonia builds up and damages the brain
118808.e: Without the urea cycle, poisonous ammonia stays in the blood. It mainly damages the brain, which can lead to confusion and even coma.
118808.m: Without urea production, ammonia poisons the brain.

118809.q: What about energy in the urea cycle?
a: It uses energy in the form of ATP
It produces a lot of ATP
It runs without any energy change
118809.e: Detoxifying ammonia costs the liver energy. Several high-energy bonds from ATP are used for every urea molecule.

118810.q: How many nitrogen atoms does a urea molecule contain?
118810.e: Urea has the formula CO(NH2)2. So it contains one carbon, one oxygen and two nitrogen atoms.
118810.m: A urea molecule contains two nitrogen atoms.

118811.q: Which chemist first made urea artificially in 1828?
118811.e: Friedrich Wöhler obtained urea from an inorganic salt. He showed that substances from living things can also be made in the lab.

118812.q: Which scientist, after whom the citric acid cycle is also named, described the urea cycle in 1932?
118812.e: In 1932 Hans Krebs discovered the urea cycle with his student Kurt Henseleit. Later he described the citric acid cycle, which is also called the Krebs cycle.
118812.m: Hans Krebs discovered the urea cycle and the citric acid cycle.

118813.q: From which molecule is bilirubin formed in the body?
118813.e: When old red blood cells are broken down, the haem from haemoglobin is released. Bilirubin is formed from it in several steps.
118813.m: Bilirubin is a breakdown product of haem.

118814.q: Why does a bruise turn greenish and then yellow over time?
a: The blood pigment is broken down step by step
The blood freezes under the skin
118814.e: In the bruise, the haem from haemoglobin is broken down. First green biliverdin forms, and from it yellow bilirubin.
118814.m: The colours of a bruise show the breakdown of the blood pigment.

118815.q: Which organ is often diseased when the skin and the whites of the eyes turn yellow because of bilirubin?
118815.e: The liver takes up bilirubin and releases it with the bile. If the liver is ill or the flow of bile is disturbed, bilirubin builds up and jaundice (icterus) develops.
118815.m: Jaundice often points to a liver problem.

118816.q: What does the liver do with bilirubin so that it can be excreted?
a: It makes it water-soluble and releases it into the bile
It turns it back into haemoglobin
It stores it permanently in fat cells
It releases it through the lungs
118816.e: In the liver, bilirubin is linked to glucuronic acid and so becomes water-soluble. That way it can reach the gut with the bile.

118817.q: How is water-insoluble, unconjugated bilirubin carried in the blood to the liver?
118817.e: Unconjugated bilirubin is fat-soluble. Albumin binds it and carries it to the liver, where it is taken up.

118818.q: What gives stools their typical brown colour?
a: Breakdown products of the bile pigment bilirubin
118818.e: Gut bacteria break down bilirubin from the bile into brown pigments such as stercobilin. If bile is missing, for example when it is blocked, the stools turn pale.
118818.m: Broken-down bilirubin colours the stools brown.

118819.q: Why do many newborn babies get mild jaundice in their first days of life?
a: Their liver still breaks down bilirubin slowly
They have too few red blood cells
118819.e: After birth, many red blood cells are broken down and a lot of bilirubin forms. The newborn's liver cannot process it fast enough yet.
118819.m: The young liver of newborns cannot keep up with the bilirubin yet.

118820.q: How is marked jaundice in newborn babies often treated?
118820.e: Blue light turns bilirubin in the skin into water-soluble forms. These can be excreted without conjugation.
118820.m: Blue light helps newborns break down bilirubin.

118821.q: What is the main job of the cytochrome P450 enzymes in the liver?
a: They break down medicines and foreign substances
118821.e: P450 enzymes change medicines and other foreign substances chemically. This makes them easier to excrete.
118821.m: P450 enzymes help the liver break down medicines.

118822.q: Why can two medicines affect each other if they are broken down by the same liver enzyme?
a: They compete for the enzyme and are broken down more slowly
They combine into sugar in the stomach
They always cancel each other out
They are then not absorbed at all
118822.e: If two drugs share the same breakdown enzyme, one can slow the breakdown of the other. Its level in the blood then rises, and side effects can occur.
118822.m: Shared breakdown enzymes can lead to interactions.

118823.q: In which organ are most medicines broken down?
118823.e: The liver contains many enzymes that change medicines. The breakdown products are then excreted through the kidneys or the bile.
118823.m: The liver breaks down most medicines.

118824.q: What happens if a liver enzyme that breaks down a medicine is blocked?
a: The medicine works more strongly and for longer
The medicine no longer works at all
The medicine turns into a vitamin
118824.e: If the breakdown enzyme is slowed, more of the drug stays in the blood for longer. This can increase the effect and the side effects.
118824.m: Blocked breakdown raises the drug level in the blood.

118825.q: Which food blocks CYP3A4 in the gut wall and can increase the effect of some medicines?
118825.e: Furanocoumarins from grapefruit block CYP3A4 permanently. As a result, more of the drug gets into the blood.
118825.m: Grapefruit juice can increase the effect of medicines.

118826.q: Why does the liver chemically change fat-soluble foreign substances?
a: So that they become water-soluble and can be excreted
So that they are stored in fatty tissue
So that they work more strongly
So that they are turned into muscle
118826.e: Fat-soluble substances are hard to excrete in urine. The liver, for example, attaches oxygen to them and makes them more water-soluble.
118826.m: The liver makes foreign substances water-soluble for excretion.

118827.q: What is it called when a substance such as St John's wort increases the production of P450 enzymes?
118827.e: In induction, more enzyme is made. As a result, other medicines are broken down faster and may work less well.
118827.m: Enzyme induction speeds up the breakdown of medicines.

118828.q: Which organ breaks down most of the alcohol in the body?
118828.e: Over 90 per cent of alcohol is broken down in the liver. Only a small part leaves the body through breath, sweat and urine.
118828.m: Alcohol is mainly broken down in the liver.

118829.q: Which vessel lies at the centre of a classic liver lobule?
118829.e: Blood flows from the corners of the lobule to the middle and collects in the central vein. From there it reaches the inferior vena cava through the hepatic veins.
118829.m: The central vein lies in the middle of the liver lobule.

118830.q: Through which vessels does blood enter the liver?
a: Through the portal vein and the hepatic artery
Through the pulmonary artery and the aorta
118830.e: The liver receives nutrient-rich blood from the gut through the portal vein and oxygen-rich blood through the hepatic artery. Their branches run with a bile duct in the corners of the liver lobules (portal triad).
118830.m: The liver gets blood from the portal vein and the hepatic artery.

118831.q: What are the widened capillaries between the rows of liver cells called?
118831.e: In the sinusoids, blood from the portal vein and hepatic artery mixes. Their leaky walls make the exchange of substances easier.
118831.m: Liver sinusoids are the capillaries of the liver.

118832.q: What are the resident macrophages in the liver sinusoids called?
118832.e: Kupffer cells eat bacteria, cell debris and old red blood cells from the portal vein blood. They are considered the largest group of resident macrophages in the body.
118832.m: Kupffer cells are the scavenger cells of the liver.

118833.q: Why does the wall of the liver capillaries have gaps?
a: So that substances pass easily between blood and liver cells
So that blood cells get into the bile
So that the liver grows faster
118833.e: Through the gaps, blood plasma reaches a narrow gap called the space of Disse. There the liver cells take up some substances and release others.
118833.m: Capillaries with gaps make exchange of substances in the liver easier.

118834.q: Roughly what shape does a classic liver lobule have in cross-section?
118834.e: The classic liver lobule is a roughly six-sided prism. The portal areas lie at its corners.
118834.m: A liver lobule is roughly hexagonal.

118835.q: Which vitamin does the liver store in especially large amounts?
118835.e: Most of the body's vitamin A is stored in the liver, mainly in the Ito cells. With chronic damage, these cells can also form scar tissue.
118835.m: The liver is the body's big vitamin A store.

118836.q: In which direction does bile flow in the liver lobule compared with the blood?
a: The opposite way, from the middle outwards
At right angles to it, into the central vein
Not at all, it stays in the cells
118836.e: Blood flows from the portal areas to the central vein. Bile flows the other way in the bile canaliculi, to the bile ducts at the edge.
118836.m: Bile and blood flow in opposite directions in the liver lobule.

118837.q: Why does a fatty liver often go unnoticed for a long time?
a: It usually causes no complaints for a long time
118837.e: The liver has no pain fibres inside it. A fatty liver is therefore often discovered by chance in an ultrasound or because of raised liver values.
118837.m: A fatty liver causes no complaints for a long time.

118838.q: Apart from being overweight, which habit is a common cause of fatty liver?
118838.e: The liver breaks down alcohol. This produces substances that promote fat storage in the liver cells. Even regular moderate amounts can make the liver fatty.
118838.m: Alcohol is an important trigger of fatty liver.

118839.q: Which drink, in large amounts, especially promotes non-alcoholic fatty liver?
118839.e: Soft drinks contain a lot of sugar, especially fructose. The liver easily turns extra fructose into fat and stores it.
118839.m: A lot of sugar in drinks can make the liver fatty.

118840.q: In what form is the fat in a fatty liver mainly stored?
118840.e: In fatty liver, mainly triglycerides collect in fat droplets of the liver cells. They form when more fatty acids arrive than are broken down or exported.
118840.m: A fatty liver mainly stores triglycerides.

118841.q: What is a fatty liver called when inflammation with cell damage is added?
118841.e: In steatohepatitis, liver cells die and inflammatory cells move in. It can progress to scarring of the liver.
118841.m: An inflamed fatty liver is called steatohepatitis.

118842.q: Which serious long-term consequence can a progressing fatty liver disease have?
118842.e: Over years, inflammation can turn into fibrosis and finally cirrhosis. This also increases the risk of liver cancer.
118842.m: An untreated fatty liver can turn into cirrhosis.

118843.q: What are the most important risk factors for non-alcoholic fatty liver?
a: Lack of vitamin C and sunburn
118843.e: Metabolic fatty liver is closely linked to being overweight, insulin resistance and type 2 diabetes. High blood pressure and raised blood fats also play a part.
118843.m: Being overweight and diabetes favour fatty liver.

118844.q: What is the most important treatment for metabolic fatty liver?
a: Losing weight through diet and exercise
118844.e: Even losing a few per cent of body weight can clearly lower liver fat. Exercise also improves sensitivity to insulin.
118844.m: Losing weight and exercise are the best therapy for fatty liver.

118845.q: Which organ does the hepatitis B virus mainly attack?
118845.e: Hepatitis means inflammation of the liver. The hepatitis B virus multiplies in the liver cells and can damage the liver permanently.
118845.m: The hepatitis B virus attacks the liver.

118846.q: What is the most effective protection against hepatitis B in Switzerland?
a: A vaccination, ideally as a baby or teenager
None, because there is no vaccine
118846.e: The FOPH recommends the hepatitis B vaccination for all babies and for teenagers who have not yet been vaccinated. It protects very reliably.
118846.m: A vaccination protects against hepatitis B.

118847.q: How do you check whether a hepatitis B vaccination has worked?
a: You measure the antibodies in the blood
You take an X-ray of the liver
118847.e: After the vaccination, the body makes antibodies against the virus. If their level in the blood is high enough, you are considered protected.
118847.m: Antibodies in the blood show vaccine protection.

118848.q: Why can you not get hepatitis B from the hepatitis B vaccination?
a: It contains only one part of the virus coat, not a whole virus
It only works after ten years
118848.e: The vaccine contains only one protein from the virus coat. The immune system learns from it to recognise the virus, but an infection is impossible.
118848.m: The hepatitis B vaccine contains no virus that can multiply.

118849.q: In whom does a hepatitis B infection especially often become chronic?
118849.e: The immune system of babies usually cannot get rid of the virus. In adults, on the other hand, the infection usually heals.
118849.m: In babies, hepatitis B especially often becomes chronic.

118850.q: Which serious long-term consequences can chronic hepatitis B have?
a: Cirrhosis of the liver and liver cell cancer
118850.e: The constant inflammation leads to scarring of the liver. In addition, the risk of hepatocellular carcinoma rises sharply.
118850.m: Chronic hepatitis B can lead to cirrhosis and liver cancer.

118851.q: Through which route, among others, is the hepatitis B virus passed on?
a: Through blood, for example via shared syringes
118851.e: The virus is present in the blood in high concentration and is very contagious. Even tiny amounts of blood on needles can cause an infection.
118851.m: Hepatitis B is passed on mainly through blood and body fluids.

118852.q: Why do antibiotics not help against hepatitis B?
a: Because hepatitis B is caused by a virus
Because the liver breaks down antibiotics immediately
Because hepatitis B is an allergy
Because antibiotics only work in children
118852.e: Antibiotics only work against bacteria. Against viruses such as the hepatitis B virus, antiviral medicines are needed.
118852.m: Antibiotics do not work against viruses.

118853.q: Which organ can become scarred over years in chronic hepatitis C?
118853.e: The hepatitis C virus often inflames the liver unnoticed for years. This can lead to cirrhosis of the liver.
118853.m: Hepatitis C can scar the liver.

118854.q: Which statement about vaccination against hepatitis C is true (as of 2025)?
a: It is part of the measles vaccination
A single dose protects for life
118854.e: Because the virus changes so much, no vaccine has been approved so far. Protection comes mainly from avoiding contact with blood and treating infected people.
118854.m: There is no vaccine against hepatitis C yet.

118855.q: Which medicines are mostly used to cure hepatitis C today?
118855.e: Direct-acting antivirals (DAAs) specifically block virus proteins. Treatment usually lasts 8 to 12 weeks.

118856.q: What is the cure rate for hepatitis C with modern direct-acting antivirals?
118856.e: With today's combination therapies, the virus is permanently removed in well over 90 per cent of patients. Earlier interferon therapies were much less effective.
118856.m: Hepatitis C can almost always be cured today.

118857.q: What did the discovery of the hepatitis C virus, honoured with the Nobel Prize in 2020, make possible?
a: Blood tests for blood donations and targeted medicines
118857.e: Since the virus has been known, blood donations can be tested for it. Medicines have also been developed that now almost always cure hepatitis C.
118857.m: The discovery of the hepatitis C virus made blood tests and cures possible.

118858.q: How does a hepatitis C infection often progress without treatment?
a: It becomes chronic in a large share of infected people
It always heals within a week
It always causes a high fever
118858.e: In most infected people, the virus stays in the body permanently. The infection often goes on for years with almost no complaints.
118858.m: Hepatitis C often becomes chronic without being noticed.

118859.q: What is the most important way the hepatitis C virus is passed on in Switzerland?
a: Blood contact, for example when sharing syringes
118859.e: Hepatitis C is passed on almost only through blood. Today this mainly concerns sharing injecting equipment when using drugs.
118859.m: Hepatitis C is passed on mainly through blood.

118860.q: How long does a modern treatment for hepatitis C usually last?
118860.e: Modern antiviral tablets are usually taken for 8 to 12 weeks. Afterwards the virus is gone in the vast majority of patients.
118860.m: Hepatitis C can be cured in a few weeks today.

118861.q: Which enzyme in the blood is most specific for damage to liver cells?
118861.e: Alanine aminotransferase is found mainly in the cytoplasm of liver cells. When the cells are damaged, it passes into the blood.
118861.m: ALT is the most typical liver cell value.

118862.q: For which causes is gamma-GT in the blood typically raised?
a: Drinking alcohol and blocked bile flow
118862.e: Gamma-glutamyl transferase reacts sensitively to alcohol and cholestasis. It is therefore a common screening value.
118862.m: A raised gamma-GT often points to alcohol or blocked bile flow.

118863.q: Which lab value typically rises together with gamma-GT when bile flow is blocked?
118863.e: In cholestasis, more alkaline phosphatase is made in the bile ducts. However, it can also come from bone.
118863.m: Alkaline phosphatase and gamma-GT show blocked bile flow.

118864.q: Why should you not do hard sport before a blood test for liver values?
118864.e: Intense exercise releases enzymes from the muscles, including AST. A raised value could then wrongly be read as liver damage; the De Ritis ratio of AST to ALT helps to interpret it.
118864.m: Hard sport can distort liver values such as AST.

118865.q: Which clotting value quickly shows that the liver is producing less?
118865.e: Many clotting factors are made in the liver and have a short half-life. If the liver produces less, the Quick value falls and the INR rises.
118865.m: The prothrombin time shows how well the liver is producing.

118866.q: Which blood protein is made in the liver and falls in chronic liver failure?
118866.e: Albumin is the most common plasma protein and is made by the hepatocytes. Because of its long half-life, it only falls when the liver has been weak for a longer time.
118866.m: Low albumin can show chronic liver weakness.

118867.q: Why is AST less specific to the liver than ALT?
a: Because it is also plentiful in heart and skeletal muscle
Because it is made only in the brain
Because it never gets into the blood
118867.e: Aspartate aminotransferase is found in many tissues, especially in muscle cells. A raised AST can therefore also come from muscle damage.
118867.m: AST can also come from muscles.

118868.q: Why do low levels of albumin and clotting factors show a weakened liver?
a: The liver breaks these proteins down
These proteins are made in the kidney
118868.e: The liver makes many blood proteins, such as albumin, clotting factors and cholinesterase. If their levels fall, the liver's production is limited.
118868.m: Low liver-made blood proteins show weak liver production.

118869.q: What made liver transplantation a successful treatment from the 1980s onwards?
118869.e: Thomas Starzl attempted the first liver transplant in 1963, but many recipients rejected the organ. Only with ciclosporin from the early 1980s did many survive long-term.
118869.m: Medicines against rejection made transplants successful.

118870.q: Why can a living person also donate for a liver transplant?
a: Because part of the liver can be removed and grows back
Because the liver is not needed for life
Because only the gall bladder is transplanted
118870.e: The liver has a great ability to regenerate. After part of it is removed, the liver parts grow back considerably in both donor and recipient.
118870.m: The liver can grow back after part of it is removed.

118871.q: Which foundation runs the national allocation of donor organs in Switzerland?
118871.e: Swisstransplant runs the national allocation office on behalf of the Confederation. For the liver, urgency counts most, measured with the MELD score.
118871.m: Swisstransplant allocates donor organs in Switzerland.

118872.q: Which visible sign of liver disease goes with a high bilirubin level?
118872.e: Bilirubin is a yellow breakdown product of the red blood pigment, which the liver excretes. It is also one of the values in the MELD score, together with INR and creatinine.
118872.m: A high bilirubin level turns skin and eyes yellow.

118873.q: Where is a donor liver usually placed during a transplant?
a: In the place of the removed diseased liver
In the pelvis next to the bladder
Under the skin of the thigh
In the chest, next to the old liver
118873.e: The diseased liver is removed and the donor liver is put in its place. Experts call this orthotopic, meaning “in the right place”. Kidneys, on the other hand, are usually placed in the pelvis.
118873.m: The donor liver usually goes in the place of the old liver.

118874.q: Why is a liver transplant for liver cancer only an option in early stages?
a: Because otherwise the cancer keeps growing despite the new liver
Because otherwise the donor liver is too small
Because large tumours do not allow anaesthesia
118874.e: If the cancer has already spread, it keeps growing despite the new liver, especially as the medicines against rejection weaken the immune defences. The Milan criteria set how large and how many the tumours may be.
118874.m: For liver cancer, a transplant only helps early on.

118875.q: Which medicines do recipients of a donor liver usually have to take for life?
a: Blood pressure lowerers such as ramipril
118875.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ and would reject it. Immunosuppressants damp down this reaction.
118875.m: After a transplant, immunosuppressants prevent rejection.

118876.q: What happens in newborn babies with blocked bile ducts (biliary atresia)?
a: Bile builds up and the liver scars
The stomach no longer makes acid
118876.e: In biliary atresia, bile cannot drain away. The children turn yellow and the liver scars quickly; this is the most common reason for liver transplants in children.
118876.m: Blocked bile ducts damage the liver of newborns.

118877.q: What is a transplant called in which a donor liver is divided and supplies two recipients?
118877.e: In a split liver, the organ is usually divided into a smaller left part for a child and a larger right part for an adult. That way one donor organ helps two people.
118877.m: A split liver supplies two recipients.

118878.q: What does ammonia in the human body mainly come from?
a: From the breakdown of amino acids
From the breakdown of fatty acids
118878.e: When amino acids are broken down, the amino group is released as ammonia. Gut bacteria also make ammonia from protein.
118878.m: Ammonia is produced when amino acids are broken down.

118879.q: Which condition arises when a lot of ammonia reaches the brain in liver failure?
118879.e: Ammonia is toxic to nerve cells and astrocytes. It causes confusion, drowsiness and, in the worst case, coma.
118879.m: Too much ammonia damages the brain.

118880.q: In which organ is poisonous ammonia turned into urea?
118880.e: The liver converts ammonia into harmless urea in the urea cycle. This is then excreted through the kidneys.
118880.m: The liver turns ammonia into urea.

118881.q: How does the urea made from ammonia mainly leave the body?
118881.e: Urea dissolves well in water and is filtered from the blood by the kidneys. It is the most important nitrogen-containing component of urine.

118882.q: Which amino acid is the most important harmless way to transport ammonia in the blood?
118882.e: Many tissues attach ammonia to glutamate and release glutamine into the blood. In the liver and kidney, the nitrogen is released again.
118882.m: Glutamine carries ammonia safely through the blood.

118883.q: Which enzyme attaches ammonia to glutamate?
118883.e: Glutamine synthetase uses ATP and makes glutamine from glutamate and ammonia.
118883.m: Glutamine synthetase detoxifies ammonia into glutamine.

118884.q: In what form is ammonia mainly found in the blood at normal pH?
118884.e: The pKa of ammonium is about 9.2. At a blood pH of 7.4, by far the largest part is therefore protonated.
118884.m: In the blood, ammonia is mostly present as ammonium.

118885.q: Which organ excretes ammonium and so helps remove acid from the body?
118885.e: The kidney tubules make ammonia from glutamine, which binds protons in the urine. In this way acids are excreted as ammonium.
118885.m: The kidney also excretes acid as ammonium.

119185.q: What is a glomerulus in the kidney?
a: A tangle of fine blood vessels
A hormone gland on the kidney
119185.e: The glomerulus is a tangle of capillaries at the start of each nephron. This is where primary urine is filtered out of the blood.
119185.m: The glomerulus is the filter tangle of the kidney.

119186.q: What is formed when fluid from the blood is filtered in the glomerulus?
119186.e: In the glomerulus, water and small dissolved substances are pressed out of the blood. This primary urine is then greatly concentrated in the kidney tubules.
119186.m: Primary urine is formed in the glomerulus.

119187.q: What are the glomerulus and Bowman's capsule called together?
119187.e: The glomerulus and Bowman's capsule together form the renal corpuscle, also called the Malpighian corpuscle. It is the start of every nephron.
119187.m: Every nephron begins with a renal corpuscle.

119188.q: What is the smallest working unit of the kidney, which begins with the glomerulus, called?
119188.e: Each kidney contains around a million nephrons. A nephron consists of the renal corpuscle and a long kidney tubule.
119188.m: The nephron is the working unit of the kidney.

119189.q: Why do red blood cells not normally get into the primary urine?
a: They are too big for the kidney filter
They are dissolved in the glomerulus
They get stuck in the bladder
119189.e: The filter in the glomerulus only lets water and small particles through. Blood cells and large proteins stay in the blood.
119189.m: The kidney filter holds back blood cells and large proteins.

119190.q: What mainly drives filtration in the glomerulus?
a: The blood pressure in the capillaries
The muscle work of Bowman's capsule
The pressure in the renal pelvis
119190.e: The hydrostatic pressure in the glomerular capillaries presses water and small particles into the inside of the capsule. The colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins works against it.
119190.m: Blood pressure pushes the filtrate out of the glomerulus.

119191.q: Roughly how many glomeruli does a human kidney have?
119191.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons, each with its own glomerulus. Together this gives a very large filter surface.
119191.m: Each kidney has around a million filter tangles.

119192.q: What is an inflammation of the glomeruli called?
119192.e: In glomerulonephritis, the filter tangles are inflamed, often because the immune system reacts wrongly. Blood and protein in the urine are typical.
119192.m: Glomerulonephritis is an inflammation of the kidney filters.

119193.q: A lot of protein is found in a urine sample. What can this point to?
a: You have drunk too much water
The liver is working especially well
119193.e: A healthy glomerulus keeps large proteins in the blood. A lot of protein in the urine therefore suggests a damaged kidney filter.
119193.m: Protein in the urine can be a sign of a damaged kidney filter.

119194.q: Roughly what percentage of primary urine is taken back into the blood?
119194.e: Of around 180 litres of primary urine, only about 1.5 litres of final urine remain. So about 99 per cent is reabsorbed.
119194.m: Almost all primary urine returns to the blood.

119195.q: What is primary urine most similar to in its make-up?
119195.e: Primary urine contains water, salts, glucose, amino acids and urea in almost the same concentration as plasma. Blood cells and large proteins are missing.
119195.m: Primary urine is blood plasma almost without protein.

119196.q: Which substance in primary urine is reabsorbed almost completely in healthy people?
119196.e: Glucose is taken back into the blood almost completely in the proximal tubule. Healthy final urine therefore contains hardly any sugar.
119196.m: Healthy urine contains practically no glucose.

119197.q: Why is sugar often found in the urine in untreated diabetes?
a: The kidneys can no longer take back all the glucose
The liver releases sugar directly into the bladder
Primary urine normally contains no sugar
119197.e: The transporters in the tubule can only take back a certain amount of glucose. If blood sugar is too high, they are overloaded and the rest ends up in the urine.
119197.m: When blood sugar is too high, sugar ends up in the urine.

119198.q: In which section of the nephron is most of the primary urine reabsorbed?
119198.e: The proximal tubule takes back about two thirds of the water and sodium. Its cells carry a brush border that enlarges the surface.
119198.m: The proximal tubule does the main work of reabsorption.

119199.q: What is the process called in which substances from primary urine return to the blood?
119199.e: In reabsorption, tubule cells take up substances from the urine and pass them to the blood. Secretion is the opposite route, from blood into urine.
119199.m: Reabsorption takes valuable substances back from the urine.

119200.q: How is glucose taken up from primary urine in the proximal tubule?
119200.e: Sodium-glucose cotransporters (SGLT) use the sodium gradient to take glucose along. The gradient is created by the sodium-potassium pump, which is why it is called secondary active transport.
119200.m: In the tubule, glucose travels together with sodium.

119201.q: How does primary urine compare osmotically with blood plasma?
a: It is four times more concentrated
119201.e: Water and small dissolved particles are filtered in the same proportion. That is why primary urine has almost the same osmolarity as plasma, around 290 mosmol/l.
119201.m: At first, primary urine is just as concentrated as plasma.

119202.q: Which principle does the loop of Henle use to concentrate urine?
119202.e: The descending and ascending limbs lie side by side and fluid flows through them in opposite directions. This builds up a strong concentration gradient in the kidney medulla.
119202.m: The loop of Henle works on the countercurrent principle.

119203.q: Which part of the loop of Henle is practically impermeable to water?
119203.e: The ascending limb pumps salt into the tissue but does not let water follow. This makes the kidney medulla salty.
119203.m: The ascending limb releases salt, but no water.

119204.q: What happens in the descending limb of the loop of Henle?
a: Water leaves into the kidney medulla by osmosis
Glucose is released into the urine
119204.e: The descending limb lets water through easily. Because the surrounding medulla is salty, water flows out and the urine becomes more concentrated.
119204.m: In the descending limb, water leaves the urine.

119205.q: What does the ascending limb of the loop of Henle release into the surrounding kidney medulla?
119205.e: The ascending limb actively transports salt out of the urine into the tissue. This creates a high salt concentration in the kidney medulla.
119205.m: The ascending limb makes the kidney medulla salty.

119206.q: What do water tablets that block salt transport in the loop of Henle do?
a: The amount of urine rises sharply
The amount of urine falls sharply
119206.e: If more salt stays in the urine, it pulls water with it. As a result, more urine is passed and the body loses water.
119206.m: Water tablets acting on the loop of Henle increase the amount of urine.

119207.q: In which part of the kidney are the loops of Henle mainly found?
119207.e: The loops dip from the cortex down into the medulla, especially deep in the nephrons close to the medulla. There they build up the concentration gradient.
119207.m: The loops of Henle reach deep into the kidney medulla.

119208.q: What use is the loop of Henle to the body?
a: It helps save water and make concentrated urine
It stores urine until it is passed
119208.e: Thanks to the loop of Henle, the kidney can remove a lot of water from the urine. That way the body loses little fluid even when you are thirsty.
119208.m: The loop of Henle helps the body save water.

119209.q: How is the loop of Henle in the kidney built?
a: As a U-shaped loop with a descending and an ascending limb
As a spiral around the renal artery
119209.e: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped section of the kidney tubule. It dips down into the kidney medulla and comes back up again.
119209.m: The loop of Henle is a hairpin-shaped loop of the kidney tubule.

119210.q: At the end of the ascending limb, how does the tubular fluid compare with blood plasma?
a: The same as final urine when thirsty
119210.e: Because the ascending limb removes salt but not water, the fluid afterwards is more dilute than plasma. That is why it is also called the diluting segment.
119210.m: The ascending limb dilutes the urine.

119211.q: Which hormone makes the collecting ducts of the kidney more permeable to water?
119211.e: When water is short, the pituitary gland releases ADH. It makes water channels be built into the collecting duct cells, so more water returns to the body.
119211.m: ADH helps the kidney save water.

119212.q: Which hormone from the adrenal cortex promotes the recovery of sodium in the kidney?
119212.e: Aldosterone acts on the collecting duct. It lets more sodium return to the blood and more potassium be excreted. In this way it also affects blood pressure.
119212.m: Aldosterone keeps salt in the body.

119213.q: Besides water balance, what other job does the kidney have?
a: It helps set the pH of the blood
It makes the red blood cells
It stores glycogen for the muscles
119213.e: The kidney can excrete acid or hold back bases. Part of this fine regulation takes place in the collecting ducts.
119213.m: The kidney also regulates the acid-base balance.

119214.q: What happens to the urine in the collecting duct when the body needs to save water?
119214.e: When water is short, the collecting duct becomes permeable to water. Water flows into the salty medulla, and the urine becomes dark and concentrated.
119214.m: When you are thirsty, the collecting duct concentrates the urine.

119215.q: Where does urine flow after it has left the collecting ducts?
119215.e: The collecting ducts open into the renal pelvis. From there, urine flows through the ureter into the bladder.
119215.m: From the collecting ducts, urine reaches the renal pelvis.

119216.q: Which section passes into the collecting duct through a connecting tubule?
119216.e: After the loop of Henle comes the distal tubule. Through the connecting tubule, several nephrons open into a shared collecting duct.
119216.m: Several nephrons share one collecting duct.

119217.q: Roughly how many nephrons does a human kidney contain?
119217.e: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Several of them open into a shared collecting duct.
119217.m: A kidney has around a million nephrons.

119218.q: How do medicines that make you pass more urine, so-called diuretics, work?
a: They make the kidney excrete more salt and water
119218.e: Diuretics block the recovery of sodium in the kidney. More water is excreted along with the salt. They are used, for example, for high blood pressure.
119218.m: Diuretics flush out salt and water.

119219.e: ADH is made by nerve cells in the hypothalamus. It travels along their nerve fibres into the pituitary gland.
119219.m: ADH is made in the hypothalamus.

119220.q: Where is ADH released into the blood?
119220.e: The posterior pituitary stores ADH and releases it into the blood when needed. It does not make the hormone itself.
119220.m: The posterior pituitary releases ADH into the blood.

119221.q: What is the second name of antidiuretic hormone?
119221.e: ADH is also called vasopressin because in high concentrations it narrows blood vessels. “Antidiuretic” means that it reduces the amount of urine.
119221.m: ADH and vasopressin are the same hormone.

119222.q: Which stimulus mainly triggers the release of ADH?
a: A drop in the potassium level
119222.e: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus report when the blood becomes too concentrated. A sharp fall in blood volume also promotes the release.
119222.m: Concentrated blood calls ADH into action.

119223.q: How does alcohol affect the release of ADH?
a: It blocks it, so you have to pass more urine
It increases it, so you pass less urine
It has no effect on it at all
119223.e: Alcohol slows the release of ADH. The kidneys then excrete more water, which can contribute to fluid loss and thirst.
119223.m: Alcohol blocks ADH and makes you pass more urine.

119224.q: Which disease arises when too little ADH is made?
119224.e: Without ADH, the kidney cannot concentrate urine; people affected pass many litres of dilute urine and are very thirsty. Since 2022, an international expert group has proposed a new name that directly names the hormone deficiency.
119224.m: If ADH is missing, a great deal of dilute urine flows.

119225.q: How does ADH make sure more water is recovered in the collecting ducts of the kidney?
a: It makes water channels be built into the cell walls
It turns urine into blood plasma
119225.e: ADH makes the cells of the collecting ducts build water channels, called aquaporins, into their membrane. As a result, more water flows from the urine back into the blood.
119225.m: ADH opens water channels in the kidney.

119226.q: Which class of substances does ADH belong to?
a: Peptide hormone made of nine amino acids
119226.e: ADH is a short peptide of nine amino acids. It is closely related to oxytocin, which also consists of nine amino acids.
119226.m: ADH is a small peptide hormone.

119227.q: Which group of hormones does aldosterone belong to?
119227.e: Aldosterone is a steroid hormone that controls the mineral balance. That is why it counts as a mineralocorticoid.
119227.m: Aldosterone is the most important mineralocorticoid.

119228.q: Which rise in the blood directly stimulates the adrenal gland to make aldosterone?
119228.e: Besides angiotensin II, a high potassium level is the strongest direct stimulus. Aldosterone then makes sure that more potassium is excreted.
119228.m: A lot of potassium in the blood increases aldosterone production.

119229.q: In which organ does aldosterone mainly act?
119229.e: In the kidney, aldosterone makes sure more sodium is recovered and more potassium is excreted. Water stays in the body along with the sodium.
119229.m: Aldosterone mainly acts in the kidney.

119230.q: Through which type of receptor does aldosterone act?
a: Through a receptor inside the cell
Through a G protein receptor in the membrane
119230.e: As a fat-soluble steroid, aldosterone enters the cell and binds to a receptor in the cytoplasm. This moves into the nucleus and acts there on reading the genes.
119230.m: Aldosterone changes how genes are read in the nucleus.

120027.q: What was special about the brain of Kim Peek, the real person behind the film “Rain Man”?
a: He had only one brain hemisphere
120027.e: Kim Peek was born with agenesis of the corpus callosum, meaning without a corpus callosum. He had an extraordinary memory for thousands of books.
120027.m: Kim Peek lived without a corpus callosum and had an enormous memory.

120028.q: What is the corpus callosum mainly made of?
120028.e: The corpus callosum is made of nerve fibres wrapped in a fatty myelin layer. This makes the tissue look white.
120028.m: The corpus callosum is a large bundle of white matter.

120029.q: Who is Broca's area named after?
120029.e: In 1861 the French doctor Paul Broca described a patient who had lost the ability to speak and had damage in the left frontal lobe. The region has carried his name ever since.
120029.m: In 1861 Paul Broca found a speech centre in the frontal lobe.

120030.q: In which brain hemisphere is Broca's area located in most right-handed people?
120030.e: In over 90 per cent of right-handed people, language is mainly based in the left hemisphere. Broca's area lies there in the lower frontal lobe.
120030.m: In most people, language sits on the left.

120031.q: What could Broca's famous patient still do fairly well despite losing his speech?
120031.e: The patient could hardly speak any more but understood much of what was said to him. From this Broca concluded that speaking is controlled by its own area of the brain.
120031.m: When Broca's area is damaged, understanding is often preserved.

120032.q: How does a person with Broca's aphasia typically speak?
120032.e: In Broca's aphasia, producing speech is a struggle and there is little grammar. Understanding language, on the other hand, is usually fairly well preserved.
120032.m: In Broca's aphasia, speaking is laborious and choppy.

120033.q: Which language centre is mainly responsible for understanding language?
120033.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls speaking. Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe is especially important for understanding language.

120034.q: Because of its main disorder, what is Broca's aphasia also called?
120034.e: Broca's aphasia mainly affects the production of speech. That is why it is also called motor or expressive aphasia.
120034.m: Broca's aphasia mainly disturbs speaking itself.

120035.q: What is the most common cause of a sudden loss of language (aphasia) in adults?
120035.e: In a stroke, part of the brain no longer receives blood. If it hits the language centres in the left hemisphere, aphasia can suddenly occur.
120035.m: A stroke can suddenly take away a person's language.

120036.q: What is the leaving out of function words and endings, typical of Broca's aphasia, called?
120036.e: In agrammatism, sentences consist mainly of content words, such as “Me hospital go”. Small words and grammatical endings are missing.
120036.m: Agrammatism is language without the building blocks of grammar.

120037.q: Which doctor described the language centre in the temporal lobe named after him in 1874?
120037.e: In 1874 the German neurologist Carl Wernicke described patients who spoke fluently but hardly understood language. He linked this to a region in the temporal lobe.
120037.m: Carl Wernicke discovered the centre for understanding language.

a: In the rear part of the upper temporal gyrus
In the occipital lobe near the visual cortex
120038.e: Wernicke's area usually lies in the left hemisphere in the rear section of the superior temporal gyrus, close to the auditory cortex.
120038.m: Wernicke's area lies near the auditory cortex in the temporal lobe.

a: A language disorder after brain damage
120039.e: In aphasia, understanding, speaking, reading or writing are disturbed because language centres in the brain are damaged. The voice and hearing are usually fine.
120039.m: Aphasia is a language disorder caused by brain damage.

120040.q: How does a person with Wernicke's aphasia typically speak?
120040.e: In Wernicke's aphasia, speech flows but contains wrong or invented words. Those affected often do not notice their mistakes because their understanding is impaired.
120040.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, people say a lot but little of it makes sense.

120041.q: What is a common cause of Wernicke's aphasia?
120041.e: Usually a stroke damages the language centre in the temporal lobe. With a broken jaw or diseased vocal cords, only the mechanics of speaking are disturbed, not the understanding of language.
120041.m: Wernicke's aphasia is often caused by a stroke.

120042.q: Which second language centre is mainly responsible for speaking?
120042.e: Broca's area in the frontal lobe mainly controls the production of speech. Wernicke's area, by contrast, is important for understanding language.
120042.m: Broca stands for speaking, Wernicke for understanding.

120043.q: In which brain hemisphere are the language centres located in most people?
120043.e: In most right-handed people and also in many left-handed people, Broca's and Wernicke's areas lie in the left hemisphere.
120043.m: The language centres are usually in the left hemisphere.

120044.q: What does a person with Wernicke's aphasia find especially difficult?
120044.e: Wernicke's area is responsible for understanding language. If it is damaged, those affected understand poorly what they hear, even though their hearing is good.
120044.m: In Wernicke's aphasia, mainly understanding is impaired.

120045.q: Who is Alzheimer's disease named after?
120045.e: In 1906 the German psychiatrist Alois Alzheimer described the typical changes in the brain of a patient with severe forgetfulness.
120045.m: Alzheimer's disease bears the name of Alois Alzheimer.

120046.q: Which deposits outside the nerve cells are typical of Alzheimer's disease?
